title: Properties & Delegation
scopeHtml: Scope: backing fields, backing properties, getters, const/top-level properties, lazy, standard and custom delegates, class delegation, Android property delegates (A1-Q161 to A1-Q185).

notes.title: Backing fields and the field keyword
notes.html:
The idea. In Kotlin a "property" is not a variable. It is a name with a getter and (for var) a setter. Sometimes the property also owns a hidden variable to store its value. That hidden variable is the backing field. Inside a custom getter or setter you reach it with the special name field.

var name: String = ""
    set(value) {
        field = value.trim()      // `field` = the hidden variable
    }

When does a backing field exist? The compiler generates one if (a) you use the default getter or setter, or (b) your custom accessor mentions field. If neither, there is no storage at all:

val isEmpty: Boolean get() = size == 0     // no field, computed each time
var counter: Int = 0
    set(value) { counter = value }         // BUG: calls the setter again -> StackOverflowError

The second example is a classic: writing counter = value inside the setter calls the setter recursively, until StackOverflowError. You must write field = value.

Decompiled.

private String name = "";
public final String getName() { return this.name; }
public final void setName(String value) { this.name = StringsKt.trim(value).toString(); }

Rules. field is only visible inside accessors of that property. A property with a backing field must be initialised (or be lateinit/abstract). Kotlin 2.x is previewing "explicit backing fields" (a different field syntax for exposing a mutable type privately); confirm in the current docs before relying on it.

Real-world. Validation or normalisation setters (email = value.lowercase()), View wrappers that push to the UI inside the setter, SharedPreferences helpers, Room entities with computed getters (Room sees the field; computed properties without a backing field are not columns unless @Ignored... confirm in docs; a getter-only property is not stored).

Real-life picture. A mailbox (property) with a flap; the box behind the flap (field) is where the letters actually sit. A "virtual" mailbox has a flap but no box: when you ask, someone computes the answer.

Common interview traps.

  • Setting the property itself inside its setter (infinite recursion).
  • Thinking every property has a field.
  • Forgetting field is not accessible outside the accessors.

notes.title: Backing property pattern
notes.html:
The idea. You want to modify a value inside a class, but let outsiders only read it. Keep a private mutable property and expose a public read-only one that points to it. Kotlin convention: private one is named with an underscore.

class SearchViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(UiState())
    val state: StateFlow<UiState> = _state.asStateFlow()

    private val _items = mutableListOf<Item>()
    val items: List<Item> get() = _items          // custom getter, no second field
}

Why not just private set? var state: UiState; private set works for a plain value. The backing-property pattern is needed when the public type differs from the private type (StateFlow vs MutableStateFlow, LiveData vs MutableLiveData, List vs MutableList).

Mechanism. val state: StateFlow<UiState> = _state.asStateFlow() creates two fields (one per property) pointing to wrappers of the same state. Using get() = _items creates only the one field _items plus a getter getItems(). The latter is cheaper but returns the mutable list typed as List, so the caller can cast it to MutableList (leaky). asStateFlow() and toList() give safer boundaries.

Real-world. Every Android ViewModel in Google's architecture samples (NowInAndroid, Sunflower): _uiState/uiState, _events as Channel/SharedFlow, _navigation. Compose mutableStateOf with private set.

Real-life picture. A shop with a counter: staff behind the counter (private, can change stock), customers in front (public, can only look through the glass).

Common interview traps.

  • Exposing the MutableStateFlow publicly.
  • Using get() = _list and believing the caller cannot mutate (a cast can).
  • Thinking private set solves different public/private types.

notes.title: Custom getter versus initializer
notes.html:
The idea. val x = expr evaluates expr once when the object is built and stores the result. val x get() = expr evaluates expr every time you read x. Looks similar, behaves very differently.

class Screen {
    val createdAt = System.currentTimeMillis()          // fixed at construction
    val now get() = System.currentTimeMillis()          // new value each read
    val random = Random.nextInt()                       // same every time
    val randomEach get() = Random.nextInt()             // different every time
}

Spot-the-bug: getter that allocates state.

val adapter: ItemAdapter get() = ItemAdapter()          // BUG: new adapter on every access
val items: MutableList<Item> get() = mutableListOf()    // BUG: always an empty fresh list
recycler.adapter = adapter
adapter.submitList(list)                                // submitted to a different adapter!

Symptoms: UI never updates, state "disappears", memory churn (a new object each read inside onBindViewHolder or Compose recomposition), GC jank visible in Perfetto. Fix: use an initializer (val adapter = ItemAdapter()) or by lazy.

Which to use.

  • Cheap derived value that must always be fresh: getter (val isLoggedIn get() = token != null).
  • Expensive or stateful object: initializer or lazy.
  • Remember that a getter-only property has no field (see previous section); an initializer has one.

Real-world. val isEmpty get() = list.isEmpty() in ListAdapter; binding.root type getters; the Compose stability issue where val items get() = listOf(...) creates a new list every recomposition and defeats skipping.

Real-life picture. A photo versus a live webcam: the initializer is a photo taken once; the getter is a live camera feed.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing = and get() =.
  • Allocating objects in a getter.
  • Expecting a getter-computed val to be stable for Compose or caching.

notes.title: How delegated properties compile, cost and local delegates
notes.html:
The idea. var x by Foo() means "don't store or compute x here; ask the helper object Foo() whenever someone reads or writes x". The helper is called a delegate. It needs getValue (and setValue for var) operator functions.

class Delegate {
    operator fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): String = "hi"
    operator fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, v: String) {}
}
class A { var x by Delegate() }

Decompiled (simplified).

public final class A {
    private final Delegate x$delegate = new Delegate();
    static final KProperty[] $$delegatedProperties = { Reflection.mutableProperty1(new MutablePropertyReference1Impl(A.class, "x", "getX()Ljava/lang/String;", 0)) };
    public final String getX() { return x$delegate.getValue(this, $$delegatedProperties[0]); }
    public final void setX(String v) { x$delegate.setValue(this, $$delegatedProperties[0], v); }
}

So every delegated property costs: an extra field for the delegate object, a KProperty reflection object in a static array (created once per class, which adds class-init time and memory), and one extra virtual call per access. Newer Kotlin versions avoid creating the KProperty objects in some cases (e.g. when the delegate does not need the property parameter; check your Kotlin version), but plan on a real, measurable cost: 100 delegated properties in a class used on a hot path add allocation and startup time. Android startup guides (App Startup / Baseline Profile discussions) warn about heavy by lazy and delegates on the main thread at launch.

Delegating to another property (Kotlin 1.4+): var old by this::new or var x by other::y forwards to another property, handy for renames and deprecation with no custom delegate. Local delegated properties work inside functions too: val v by lazy { compute() } as a local variable (the delegate object is created in a local variable and KProperty passed).

Real-world. by lazy, by viewModels(), by remember { }, by mutableStateOf, by preferencesDataStore, by inject() in Koin, by navArgs(), Kotlin Gradle DSL val foo by project.

Real-life picture. A personal assistant: when you ask "what's my schedule?" you don't look it up; the assistant is asked every time (extra step, but the logic lives in one place).

Common interview traps.

  • Believing delegation is free.
  • Forgetting the exact signature of getValue(thisRef, property).
  • Not knowing the $delegate field name or that reflection (KProperty) is passed in.
  • Missing delegation to another property with by ::other.

notes.title: const val, val and JvmField
notes.html:
The idea. Three ways to expose a constant-looking value, compiled very differently.

stored as getter generated? inlined at call site? can hold
const val X = 5 static final field no yes (value copied) primitives and String only; compile-time constant; top-level/object/companion
val X = ... in object/companion private static field + getter in the companion class yes no anything
@JvmField val X public static field no no anything
top-level val X static field in FileKt + getter yes no anything 
object Api {
    const val BASE = "https://api.example.com"     // inlined everywhere
    val client = OkHttpClient()                    // getClient()
    @JvmField val GSON = Gson()                    // public static GSON
}

For a companion val, Kotlin generates a private static field in the outer class plus a getter on Companion; from Java you write Foo.Companion.getBar(). With @JvmField or const it is simply Foo.BAR. @JvmStatic generates a static method in addition.

Production incident: stale const across modules. const val values are copied into every class that uses them at compile time. If module :core has const val API_VERSION = 2 and :feature uses it, then you change it to 3 and rebuild only :core (or ship :core as a pre-built AAR/library and the app uses an old copy), the app code still contains 2. Symptoms: wrong endpoint, feature flag key or database version mismatch appears only in some builds; incremental build vs clean build differ. Fixes: do a clean build, make cross-module configuration a plain val (read at runtime through the getter), or put such values in BuildConfig and only rely on the final application module. The same applies to public static final in Java and to library consumers: changing a const in a library is a source and binary behaviour change that consumers only see after recompiling.

Room version trap. @Database(version = DbConstants.VERSION) needs a const val because annotation arguments must be compile-time constants.

Real-life picture. A printed notice stuck on every classroom wall (const): if the school changes the rule, you must reprint and re-stick them all. A val is a note saying "ask the office" (always current).

Common interview traps.

  • Using const val for objects or non-primitive types (compile error).
  • Believing changing a const in one module updates the others without recompiling.
  • Not knowing @JvmField removes the getter/setter and cannot be used on private, const or properties with custom accessors or open/override.

notes.title: Top-level properties
notes.html:
The idea. In Kotlin you can declare val/var directly in a file, outside any class. They belong to the package and are accessible everywhere (subject to visibility).

// Config.kt
val DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = 30_000L
internal var debugLogging = false
private val cache = LruCache<String, Bitmap>(100)

Mechanism. They compile to static fields (private) inside a generated class named after the file (ConfigKt) with static getters/setters. Initialisation runs in that class's static initializer, the first time the file class is touched (any function or property of that file), not at app start. So a top-level property with a slow initialiser triggers its cost on the first access, potentially on the main thread. @file:JvmName("Config") renames the class; const val and @JvmField give plain public static fields.

Pitfalls.

  • Global mutable state: tests share it, process death resets it, multi-process apps have separate copies.
  • Initialisation order across files is not defined; one property can read an uninitialised (null) another through a class-init cycle (rare but real; it shows as NullPointerException in <clinit>).
  • Holding Context/View/Activity in a top-level var is a memory leak (static root; LeakCanary shows ConfigKt as GC root).
  • Class-init failures: an exception in a top-level initialiser is thrown as ExceptionInInitializerError the first time, then NoClassDefFoundError for later accesses. Crashlytics shows a confusing second crash.

Real-world. private val Context.dataStore by preferencesDataStore("settings") at top level (the official pattern: needs a single instance per file), private const val TAG = "..." for logging, Compose design tokens (val Purple200 = Color(0xFFBB86FC) in Color.kt), theme and typography files.

Real-life picture. A noticeboard in the school corridor: anyone can read it, but it is only put up when someone first walks past (lazy class load), and if someone defaces it, everyone sees.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking top-level properties initialise at app start.
  • Storing Context/Activity in them.
  • Not knowing the generated FileNameKt class.
  • Creating two preferencesDataStore for the same file (crash: "There are multiple DataStores active for the same file").

notes.title: lazy thread safety modes
notes.html:
The idea. val x by lazy { expensive() } runs expensive() the first time x is read and remembers the result. The mode controls what happens when many threads read it at the same time.

val a by lazy { create() }                                         // SYNCHRONIZED (default)
val b by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) { create() }
val c by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE) { create() }
Mode Class Behaviour Cost
SYNCHRONIZED (default) SynchronizedLazyImpl one thread runs the initialiser holding a lock (the lazy object itself); others wait; initialiser runs once volatile read + lock on first contention
PUBLICATION SafePublicationLazyImpl many threads may run the initialiser at the same time; the first one to finish wins (via compare-and-set) and all see the same value no lock, possibly wasted/duplicated work and side effects
NONE UnsafeLazyImpl no synchronisation cheapest; only safe if you are sure of a single thread

Mechanism. The value is stored in a field of the Lazy object (_value), initially an UNINITIALIZED_VALUE sentinel. The SYNCHRONIZED one uses double-checked locking with a @Volatile field. After success, the initializer lambda reference is set to null so it (and what it captured) can be garbage collected.

Which one on Android.

  • UI properties only touched on the main thread: NONE is safe and avoids the volatile read (microseconds, only matters in hot paths).
  • Shared singletons used from many threads: default.
  • Cheap idempotent initialisers (e.g. building a formatter) where deadlock must be avoided: PUBLICATION.

Real-world. Retrofit service in a repository private val api by lazy { retrofit.create<Api>() }, Json/Moshi instances, SimpleDateFormat (not thread-safe: share the lazy, but remember the value itself is not thread-safe), Application-level val database by lazy { Room.databaseBuilder(...).build() }, Hilt/Dagger Lazy<T> (a different type with similar goals).

Real-life picture. A single key to the stationery cupboard (SYNCHRONIZED): one student fetches the new box, others wait. PUBLICATION: everyone runs to the shop, the first back wins, extras are wasted. NONE: assuming only you are ever in the room.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing the lazy lambda can run twice in the default mode (it cannot; PUBLICATION can).
  • Using NONE for a value touched from several threads.
  • Thinking lazy makes the object thread-safe, only its initialisation.

notes.title: lazy failure semantics, memory and deadlocks
notes.html:
The idea. lazy has some less-known behaviours around errors, memory and locking that cause real incidents.

Failure semantics. If the initialiser throws, nothing is cached. The exception propagates to the caller and the next access runs the initialiser again (for SYNCHRONIZED and PUBLICATION). A permanently failing initialiser, for example reading a missing file, retries on every access: repeated slow work, repeated network calls, log spam, each throwing in a different place. If you want "fail once, remember it", catch inside and store a Result.

Memory. Once initialised the Lazy drops its lambda (initializer = null), so captured this/Context is released from the lambda. But the value is retained for the life of the owner. A by lazy holding a Bitmap, View or Context in a long-lived singleton stays forever. Until initialisation, the lambda holds whatever it captured.

Fragment views trap (by lazy on views).

class MyFragment : Fragment() {
    private val titleView by lazy { requireView().findViewById<TextView>(R.id.title) }
}

The first read caches the view from the first view hierarchy. After navigating away and back the Fragment instance survives, but its view is destroyed and recreated in onCreateView; titleView still points to the old, detached view. Symptoms: UI updates apply to nothing, and the old view keeps the old Activity context alive (LeakCanary: MyFragment.titleView$delegate -> TextView -> Activity (destroyed), "Fragment view not cleared after onDestroyView"). Use ViewBinding with _binding = null in onDestroyView or viewLifecycleOwner-bound properties.

Deadlock and ANR. The SYNCHRONIZED lock is held while the initialiser runs. If a lazy initialiser on thread A waits for the main thread (runBlocking(Dispatchers.Main), withContext(Main) + .get(), or reads another lazy that needs main), while the main thread is waiting for the same lazy's lock, you get a deadlock. On Android that shows up as an ANR with the main thread BLOCKED on SynchronizedLazyImpl.getValue ("waiting to lock ... held by thread N") in the ANR trace. Cyclic lazy dependencies between two singletons produce the same pattern, or StackOverflowError/the initialiser recursion calling its own lazy. Fixes: never block or switch threads inside a lazy initialiser, break cycles, use PUBLICATION, or initialise on a background thread at startup.

Real-life picture. Two people each holding one chopstick and waiting for the other: neither lets go, and the school bell (watchdog, ANR after about 5 seconds for input) rings.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a failed lazy remembers the failure.
  • Using by lazy for anything bound to a view's lifecycle.
  • Doing network or main-thread hops inside lazy.
  • Forgetting that the lock is the Lazy instance itself.

notes.title: Observable vetoable and notNull
notes.html:
The idea. The Delegates object in the stdlib provides three ready-made delegates.

var name: String by Delegates.observable("none") { prop, old, new ->
    println("${prop.name}: $old -> $new")           // runs AFTER the change
}
var age: Int by Delegates.vetoable(0) { _, old, new ->
    new >= 0                                         // returning false rejects the change
}
// no lateinit for primitives; notNull works for them
var token: String by Delegates.notNull()             // throws IllegalStateException if read before set

Details.

  • observable: callback after the value is assigned; fires even if the new value equals the old (no deduplication; add if (old != new) yourself).
  • vetoable: callback before assignment, returns Boolean; false keeps the old value silently (no exception, easy to miss).
  • notNull: for non-null types of primitives where lateinit is not allowed (lateinit cannot be used on Int/Long/Boolean); throws IllegalStateException: Property x should be initialized before get.. lateinit throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException instead.
  • None of them is thread-safe by default.

Real-world. Simple state holders pushing UI updates (var progress by observable(0) { _, _, v -> bar.progress = v }), validation of ranges (vetoable), SDK singletons that must be set by init() (var appId by notNull<Int>()).

Real-life picture. observable is a doorbell that rings after the guest has come in; vetoable is a guard who can refuse entry; notNull is an empty seat that must be filled before anyone sits.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing the observable callback fires only on change.
  • Not realising vetoable rejects silently.
  • Using lateinit on a primitive (compile error) rather than notNull.
  • Assuming thread-safety.

notes.title: Map delegation
notes.html:
The idea. A class's properties can be read from (and written to) a Map<String, Any?>, using the property name as key. Great for JSON-like or dynamic data.

class User(val map: Map<String, Any?>) {
    val name: String by map
    val age: Int by map
}
val u = User(mapOf("name" to "Asha", "age" to 25))
u.name   // "Asha"

class MutableUser(val map: MutableMap<String, Any?>) {
    var name: String by map
}

Mechanism. The stdlib provides Map<in String, V>.getValue(thisRef, property) and MutableMap.setValue as extension operators. Key = property.name. Missing key -> NoSuchElementException: Key name is missing in the map. Wrong type -> ClassCastException at the access (unchecked cast). Writing to a MutableMap delegate changes the map, which the caller can observe.

Where it fits and doesn't. Dynamic configuration, feature-flag/remote-config bags, parsing loosely typed JSON, tiny DSLs. Not for type-safe domain models: no compile-time guarantee that keys exist; renames (R8 obfuscation does not change the property name string but your map keys must match); no null handling unless the property is nullable and the key is present.

Real-world. Firebase Remote Config and Intent.extras/Bundle wrappers, ad-hoc Map<String, Any?> from Firestore documents (doc.data), Gradle scripts (val foo by extra).

Real-life picture. A pigeonhole board where each box has a name tag; the property is just "go and look in box 'age'".

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting a default for a missing key.
  • Not knowing the key equals the property name.
  • Assuming type safety at runtime.

notes.title: Class delegation with by
notes.html:
The idea. "Use another object to implement this interface" without writing every forwarding method by hand. It is Kotlin's built-in support for composition over inheritance (the decorator pattern).

interface Analytics { fun log(event: String); fun setUser(id: String) }

class LoggingAnalytics(private val inner: Analytics) : Analytics by inner {
    override fun log(event: String) {            // override only what changes
        Timber.d(event); inner.log(event)
    }
}

Mechanism. The compiler generates forwarding methods for every interface member not overridden: setUser(id) = this.$$delegate_0.setUser(id), stored in a synthetic field $$delegate_0.

Semantics and limits.

  • The delegate is not aware of the wrapper. Calls inside inner go to inner's own methods, not your overrides. If inner.log() internally calls this.setUser(), your override of setUser is not called (unlike inheritance with virtual calls). The "self" problem.
  • Only interfaces can be delegated, not classes.
  • Members of Any (equals, hashCode, toString) are not delegated automatically.
  • The delegate expression is evaluated once at construction (can be a constructor property or by Impl()).
  • With property overriding conflicts, if two interfaces have the same method you must override explicitly.

Interface evolution incident. You delegate class Cached(repo: UserRepo) : UserRepo by repo. Months later someone adds fun deleteAll() to UserRepo. Your decorator compiles and forwards automatically, bypassing the caching/auditing/permission logic you intended (e.g. the cache is never invalidated, the audit log misses deletions). A new interface method with a default implementation is even harder to notice. Post-incident actions: code review rule that any interface change checks all decorators, contract tests for decorators, explicit overrides for security-sensitive methods, or prefer sealed/small interfaces. In multi-module apps the interface owner may not see the decorators in other modules.

Real-world. Collection wrappers (class ReadOnlyList<T>(l: List<T>) : List<T> by l), OkHttp interceptors/EventListeners, Compose Modifier implementations, analytics/logging/caching repositories, ViewModelProvider.Factory decorators, Android ContextWrapper (Java version of the same idea).

Real-life picture. A receptionist who forwards all calls to the manager, except the ones she handles herself. If the manager gets a new phone line, it's forwarded too, even though you wanted to screen it.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting delegated calls to hit your overrides (they do not).
  • Delegating a class instead of an interface.
  • Not realising new interface methods are auto-forwarded.
  • Forgetting equals/hashCode/toString.

notes.title: Custom ReadOnlyProperty and ReadWriteProperty
notes.html:
The idea. You can write your own delegate to share logic across many properties. Implement ReadOnlyProperty<in T, out V> (for val) or ReadWriteProperty<in T, V> (for var); or just write the operator functions.

class PrefString(private val prefs: SharedPreferences, private val key: String, private val default: String) :
    ReadWriteProperty<Any?, String> {
    override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>) = prefs.getString(key, default) ?: default
    override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: String) =
        prefs.edit().putString(key, value).apply()
}

class Settings(prefs: SharedPreferences) {
    var username by PrefString(prefs, "username", "")
    var theme by PrefString(prefs, "theme", "light")
}

Design trade-offs for a preferences delegate.

  1. Key naming: use the property name (property.name) as the default key to avoid typos, but then renaming the property (or R8 renaming? Kotlin keeps property names for delegates because KProperty.name comes from metadata/constant strings; still, confirm) silently changes the stored key and loses user data. Prefer explicit keys for persisted data.
  2. Threading: commit() blocks on disk (can cause ANR); apply() is async but in-memory update is immediate. Reads happen on the calling thread; SharedPreferences loads the whole file on first access (can be tens of ms on main).
  3. Testing: inject SharedPreferences/DataStore through the constructor.
  4. Modern choice: prefer Jetpack DataStore (asynchronous, Flow-based) over blocking property delegates; a delegate with getValue cannot be suspend, so a DataStore-backed delegate would need runBlocking (a risk for ANRs on the main thread) or expose Flow.
  5. No change notification unless you add listeners.
  6. Cost: each delegate is an object plus reflection data (see earlier section).

Real-world. Many apps (Paytm, Swiggy-style onboarding flags) hide SharedPreferences behind by boolean(key) delegates; Android KTX's SharedPreferences.edit { }; DataStore's preferencesDataStore (a ReadOnlyProperty<Context, DataStore<Preferences>>); Koin's by inject().

Real-life picture. A standard-shaped drawer in a cabinet: each property is a labelled drawer built from one design, and the carpenter writes the drawer design once.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the thisRef type parameter (e.g. Fragment only).
  • Using the property name as a persisted key and then renaming the property.
  • Blocking calls (commit, runBlocking) inside getValue on the main thread.
  • Believing the delegate is created per access (it's per instance of the owner).

notes.title: Android delegates viewModels and navArgs
notes.html:
The idea. The AndroidX KTX libraries give delegates that fetch a scoped object lazily: by viewModels() (this Fragment/Activity scope), by activityViewModels() (the host Activity scope, shared between Fragments), by navGraphViewModels(R.id.graph) (scoped to a navigation graph's back stack entry), by navArgs<Args>() (Safe Args), plus hiltNavGraphViewModels.

class DetailFragment : Fragment() {
    private val vm: DetailViewModel by viewModels()
    private val shared: SharedViewModel by activityViewModels()
    private val flow: CheckoutViewModel by navGraphViewModels(R.id.checkout_graph) { defaultViewModelProviderFactory }
    private val args: DetailFragmentArgs by navArgs()
}

Mechanism. Each returns a Lazy<T> (ViewModelLazy, NavArgsLazy). The ViewModel is created on first access through a ViewModelProvider(store, factory). NavArgsLazy reads fragment.arguments on first access and caches the result.

Failures when accessed outside the attach window (production incident).

  • Reading viewModels() in a property initialiser or constructor works only because it's lazy; but touching it before onAttach/after onDetach throws IllegalStateException: Can't access ViewModels from detached fragment.
  • activityViewModels() needs requireActivity(): IllegalStateException: Fragment X not attached to an activity when used from a late callback (a coroutine/Retrofit callback arriving after the fragment detached) or in a lazily-run lambda.
  • navArgs() throws IllegalStateException: Fragment X has null arguments when started without the argument bundle (deep link missing params, a manual FragmentManager transaction), and navGraphViewModels throws IllegalArgumentException: No destination with ID ... is on the NavController's back stack if the graph is not currently on the back stack (e.g. process death restoring a destination in a different state, or accessing from a Fragment outside the graph).
  • Using by viewModels() inside onCreateView is fine; inside a background callback after onDestroy, creating a new ViewModel is wasted or fails.

Rules. Use delegates only between onAttach and onDetach (practically from onCreate on); use viewLifecycleOwner for observing; capture needed values early; don't resolve in a long-lived callback.

Scale / design issue: activityViewModels scope misuse. Putting everything in an activityViewModels ViewModel makes it live for the whole Activity: state from screen A (stale form values, an old selected item) leaks into screen B, memory is retained until the Activity finishes, and multiple Fragments writing the same state create hidden coupling and ordering bugs. In a single-Activity app that means essentially an app-wide singleton that is never cleared (until process or Activity death), and tests need the Activity. Prefer navGraphViewModels (cleared when the graph is popped) for flows such as checkout/onboarding, viewModels() for screen state, and pass results via the Navigation SavedStateHandle / Fragment Result API for one-off events. Clear shared state explicitly when the flow ends. Hilt's hiltNavGraphViewModels and Compose's hiltViewModel(navBackStackEntry) follow the same scoping idea.

Real-world. Google's Navigation samples, Fragment FragmentResultListener, Hilt @HiltViewModel injection with by viewModels(); large apps (Gmail, Google Play) use scoped back-stack-entry ViewModels for multi-step flows.

Real-life picture. A whiteboard in a classroom (viewModels), the school notice board everyone shares (activityViewModels), and a project folder for just one class trip that gets thrown away afterwards (navGraphViewModels). Putting every note on the school notice board makes a mess.

Common interview traps.

  • Not knowing these are Lazy and resolve on first use.
  • Using activityViewModels for everything.
  • Forgetting that navArgs needs arguments and navGraphViewModels needs the graph on the back stack.
  • Accessing from callbacks after detach.

notes.title: provideDelegate and PropertyDelegateProvider
notes.html:
The idea. Sometimes you need to check or configure things at the moment the delegate is attached to a property, not at each access, for example validate the property name or register it. provideDelegate is a hook called once when the property is declared, which returns the real delegate.

class RequireNonBlank(val msg: String) {
    operator fun provideDelegate(thisRef: Any?, prop: KProperty<*>): ReadOnlyProperty<Any?, String> {
        require(prop.name.startsWith("pref_")) { "bad name ${prop.name}" }   // runs at construction
        return ReadOnlyProperty { _, _ -> msg }
    }
}

// Same without a class (Kotlin 1.4+):
val provider = PropertyDelegateProvider<Any?, ReadOnlyProperty<Any?, String>> { _, prop ->
    ReadOnlyProperty { _, _ -> prop.name }
}

Mechanism. For val x by Foo(), the compiler generates x$delegate = Foo().provideDelegate(this, prop) and then uses the returned object's getValue. This is how the property is bound to the owner at creation time, so errors (invalid keys, duplicate registrations) show up when the object is constructed rather than at first use.

Real-world. Gradle Kotlin DSL (val myTask by tasks.registering), Koin and Kodein bindings, by preferencesDataStore-like registration, ActivityResultContracts wrappers, delegates that register the property name in a registry (analytics event schemas, Room-like bindings).

Real-life picture. A hotel check-in desk: the clerk checks your booking once when you arrive (provideDelegate), then you use the room many times without being checked again.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing provideDelegate with getValue.
  • Not knowing it runs once per property per instance, at construction time.
  • Forgetting the operator modifier.

notes.title: Delegation in Compose with remember
notes.html:
The idea. In Compose, var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) } is a normal property delegate. mutableStateOf(0) returns a MutableState<Int> object; remember keeps the same object across recompositions; the by keyword lets you write count instead of count.value.

@Composable
fun Counter() {
    var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }
    Button(onClick = { count++ }) { Text("Clicked $count") }
}

Mechanism. by works because the Compose runtime defines extension operators inline operator fun <T> State<T>.getValue(thisObj: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): T and MutableState<T>.setValue(...) in androidx.compose.runtime. You must import androidx.compose.runtime.getValue and setValue; otherwise the compiler says "Property delegate must have a 'getValue(Nothing?, KProperty<*>)' method" (the classic missing-import error). It's a local delegated property, so there is no field; a local MutableState variable and getValue/setValue calls are generated, and reads inside composition register the read with the snapshot system so the scope recomposes.

Gotchas.

  • remember loses its value on configuration change or when leaving composition; use rememberSaveable to survive rotation/process death.
  • Capturing count in a lambda that outlives composition reads the latest value because each read goes through getValue on the state object. Using val c = count first captures a stale snapshot, a common source of stale-closure bugs.
  • Writing state during composition (not in an event/effect) causes recomposition loops.
  • Use derivedStateOf for values computed from other state; remember(key) to reset.
  • by on a State from collectAsState() is similar: val ui by vm.state.collectAsState().

Real-world. Every Jetpack Compose app (Google Play, Twitter/X, Airbnb screens), Material text fields (var text by remember { mutableStateOf("") }), LazyListState via rememberLazyListState() also supports derivedStateOf.

Real-life picture. A whiteboard in a room (state) with a note "ask the board": you can say "the score" instead of "the number written on the board", and everyone watching the board re-draws their picture whenever it changes.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the getValue/setValue imports.
  • Using remember where rememberSaveable is needed.
  • Copying count into a local val inside a lambda and expecting updates.
  • Thinking by creates a field (it's a local delegate).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• A Kotlin property is a getter/setter pair; a backing field (field) exists only when the default accessor is used or field is referenced. Assigning the property inside its own setter recurses.
  • Use a private mutable property plus a public read-only one (_state/state) when public and private types differ.
  • val x = e evaluates once; val x get() = e evaluates each access, so never allocate state in a getter.
  • Delegated properties compile to a $delegate field plus KProperty metadata and forwarding calls; they cost something. provideDelegate runs once at construction.
  • const val is inlined (stale across modules without a full rebuild); @JvmField exposes a plain field; top-level properties live in FileKt and initialise on first class load.
  • lazy: SYNCHRONIZED (default, lock), PUBLICATION (races allowed), NONE (no sync). Failures are not cached, locks can deadlock into ANRs, and view-bound by lazy leaks stale views.
  • Delegates.observable/vetoable/notNull and map delegation are quick tools with silent failure modes.
  • Class delegation (: I by x) forwards interface members only, bypasses wrapper overrides inside the delegate, and auto-forwards newly added methods.
  • Custom delegates share logic (preferences); prefer DataStore for async persistence.
  • viewModels, activityViewModels, navGraphViewModels, navArgs are lazy and valid only while attached; choose the narrowest scope.
  • Compose by remember { mutableStateOf() } relies on imported getValue/setValue extensions and a local delegated property.

questions.promptHtml: What is field in a Kotlin property accessor, when does the compiler actually generate a backing field, and what goes wrong if you write set(value) { name = value }?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It shows whether you understand that a Kotlin property is a getter/setter pair plus an optional storage slot, not a Java field with sugar on top.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Kotlin property is a getter, and for a var also a setter. The JVM field behind it is optional. The compiler generates a backing field only when at least one accessor uses the default implementation, or when a custom accessor mentions field. Inside an accessor, field is the only way to reach that storage. Writing name = value inside the setter of name calls the setter again, so it recurses until you get a StackOverflowError.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• var name: String = "" compiles to a private String name field, a getName() that returns it and a setName(String) that assigns it. Callers in Kotlin and Java always go through the accessors. The only exceptions are @JvmField, const, and private properties with default accessors, where the compiler can read the field directly.
  • When does a backing field exist?
Declaration Backing field? Why
val a = 1 Yes default getter
val b get() = compute() No custom getter never mentions field
var c = 0; set(v) { field = v.coerceAtLeast(0) } Yes setter uses field, getter is default
var d get() = x; set(v) { x = v } No both accessors custom, neither uses field, so no initializer is allowed
val e by lazy { } No e field, but a e$delegate field storage lives in the delegate
  • An initializer (= ...) writes straight into the backing field. It does not run the custom setter. People get surprised when the validation in their setter is skipped for the initial value.
  • field is in scope only inside that property's own accessors. Other members of the class must go through the property.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Account {
    // BROKEN: the setter calls itself -> StackOverflowError on the first assignment
    var balance: Long = 0
        set(value) { balance = value.coerceAtLeast(0) }
}

class AccountFixed {
    var balance: Long = 0          // the initializer bypasses the setter
        set(value) {
            require(value >= 0) { "negative balance" }
            field = value          // writes the backing field directly
        }
        // the getter is default here, so the backing field is still generated
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Recursion through the property name inside its own accessor (setter or getter).
  • Expecting the initializer to go through setter validation.
  • Thinking val x get() = ... stores anything. It recomputes on every access (Q163).
  • Adding private set and assuming that makes the value immutable from outside. It only hides the setter. A mutable object behind it is still mutable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a getter use field? → Yes, for example get() = field.trim(). This is common for lazily normalising a value.
  2. Does a private property with default accessors still generate a getter method? → No. For private properties with default accessors the compiler reads the field directly, with no synthetic getter.
  3. Where does an annotation on a property land in bytecode? → Kotlin picks the first applicable target in the order constructor param, then property, then field. A Java annotation like @Inject can't target a Kotlin "property", so on @Inject lateinit var repo: Repo it lands on the field, which is what Hilt field injection needs. On a constructor val it lands on the parameter only, so write @field:X or @get:X when a tool reads fields or getters. Kotlin 2.2 started changing this defaulting rule (-Xannotation-default-target). Check the release notes for your version.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "field refers to the variable". The senior answer explains when a field exists at all, that initializers bypass setters, and how use-site annotation targets (@field:, @get:) decide where annotations land in bytecode.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A set(value) { state = value } typo in a custom View crashed on the first layout pass, but only in the code path that set the property after inflation. Previews and the happy-path test never assigned it.

questions.promptHtml: Why do Android codebases declare private val _state = MutableStateFlow(...) next to val state: StateFlow<...> = _state? What does it actually protect, and is there a language-level replacement?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the most common property idiom in modern Android. Interviewers want to see you know its guarantees and its limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It is the backing-property pattern. The class keeps the mutable type private and exposes only the read-only supertype, so only the owner can write state, which gives unidirectional data flow. It is a compile-time API boundary, not a runtime one: anyone can downcast state as MutableStateFlow and write to it. asStateFlow() closes that hole by wrapping the flow in a read-only wrapper. Kotlin 2.3 added explicit backing fields as an Experimental feature behind -Xexplicit-backing-fields. They let you declare one property with a public read-only type and a private mutable field.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Two declarations produce two members. _state is a private field with no accessor. state is a field (or a getter) returning the same object typed as StateFlow. Both point at one instance.
  • val state: StateFlow<UiState> = _state stores the same reference. val state get() = _state stores nothing and returns the same reference. Either works. = _state.asStateFlow() wraps it once in a ReadonlyStateFlow, so a downcast fails at runtime.
  • The same idea applies to MutableList vs List and MutableLiveData vs LiveData. Read-only collection types do not make the data immutable (see the collections chunk).
  • Explicit backing fields (Kotlin 2.3, Experimental):
// Requires: freeCompilerArgs += "-Xexplicit-backing-fields" (Experimental in 2.3)
class SearchViewModel : ViewModel() {
    val state: StateFlow<UiState>
        field = MutableStateFlow(UiState())

    fun onQuery(q: String) {
        state.value = state.value.copy(query = q) // smart-cast to MutableStateFlow inside the class
    }
}

Some community posts say the feature is stable in Kotlin 2.4. I have not confirmed that from official release notes, so check "What's new in Kotlin" before you use it in production code. Like _state/state, it protects only at compile time.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class CartViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _items = MutableStateFlow<List<Item>>(emptyList())
    val items: StateFlow<List<Item>> = _items.asStateFlow()   // a downcast won't give write access

    fun add(item: Item) = _items.update { it + item }        // a new list, so StateFlow emits
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• val items get() = MutableStateFlow(...). That creates a new flow on every read (see Q177).
  • Exposing _items as StateFlow<MutableList<Item>> and mutating the list in place. The reference doesn't change, so nothing emits.
  • Making _state internal or protected "for tests". Tests should drive state through public functions.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is asStateFlow() free? → It allocates one small wrapper, once, if you assign it to a val. Calling it inside a getter allocates a wrapper per read. That costs little, but it breaks identity checks.
  2. Why not just private set on a var state: UiState? → That limits who can reassign, but a plain var is not observable. You still need a flow or a snapshot state to push changes.
  3. What does the bytecode look like for val state = _state? → Two fields holding the same reference, plus a getState() getter. The field cost is negligible. The value is the API boundary.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "so the UI can't modify it". The senior answer adds that it is a compile-time boundary only, shows asStateFlow() as a runtime guard, mentions explicit backing fields and their Experimental status, and points out the in-place mutation trap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A shared Compose component downcast a public StateFlow to MutableStateFlow to "reset" a filter. Two screens then fought over the same state. After asStateFlow() made the downcast crash in debug, the author fixed the API.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between val total = items.sumOf { it.price }, val total get() = items.sumOf { it.price } and val total by lazy { items.sumOf { it.price } }?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Three similar-looking lines with three different evaluation strategies. Getting this wrong causes stale data or wasted CPU on hot paths.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The initializer runs once, during construction, and stores the result in a backing field. The custom getter has no field and recomputes on every access, so it is always fresh but costs O(n) per read. lazy computes on first access, caches the result forever, and adds a delegate object plus thread-safety overhead. Choose by asking two questions: can the inputs change after construction, and how often is the value read compared with how often it changes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Form When computed Storage Sees later changes to items? Cost per read
val total = ... constructor, in declaration order backing field No, it is a snapshot field read
val total get() = ... every access none Yes full recomputation
val total by lazy {...} first access total$delegate (Lazy) No, it is frozen at first read volatile read plus a delegate call
  • Order matters for initializers. Property initializers and init blocks run top to bottom (see K2b for init order). If val total = items.sum() is declared above items, items is still null at that point, even though its type is non-null.
  • A custom getter is the right choice for derived, cheap values over mutable inputs, like val isEmpty get() = size == 0. It is the wrong choice for anything that allocates (formatters, regexes, new flows) or does O(n) work and is read inside onBindViewHolder or composition.
  • lazy suits values that are expensive, may never be needed, and depend only on inputs that are fixed after construction.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Invoice(private val items: MutableList<Line>) {
    val snapshotTotal = items.sumOf { it.cents }           // frozen at construction
    val liveTotal get() = items.sumOf { it.cents }         // recomputed on every read
    val formatter by lazy { NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance() } // expensive, created once

    // BROKEN: allocates a Regex on every call to isValid(...)
    val emailRegex get() = Regex("^[^@]+@[^@]+$")
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using lazy for a value whose inputs change, which gives a stale cache.
  • Using a getter that allocates on every read inside a 60 fps path.
  • Assuming a getter is "free" because it looks like a field access. Java callers see getTotal(), and so do profilers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a val return different values on each read? → Yes. val means "no setter", not "constant". A custom getter or a delegate can return anything.
  2. How do you cache a derived value but invalidate it when the input changes? → Recompute in the setter of the input (set(v) { field = v; total = ... }), or model it as a derived flow with map/stateIn so it is reactive.
  3. Is lazy on a data class property included in equals? → Only primary-constructor properties take part in equals, so no. Also note that copy() creates a fresh, uninitialized lazy.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer explains "once vs every time". The senior answer adds the staleness vs cost trade-off, initialization order (a non-null property that is null during construction), and how val doesn't mean immutable.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A val displayPrice get() = NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(locale).format(...) inside a list item model showed up in an allocation trace as about 1k formatter instances per second during fast scroll. Moving the formatter to a single cached instance fixed the jank.

questions.promptHtml: What does val x: T by something compile to? What does the delegate object need to provide?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every Android delegate (by viewModels, by lazy, by remember, by navArgs) is built on this. Senior candidates can explain it with no magic.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The compiler creates a hidden field, x$delegate, that holds the result of the expression after by. It then generates a getter that calls x$delegate.getValue(this, ::x), and for a var a setter that calls setValue(this, ::x, value). The delegate needs operator fun getValue(thisRef, property: KProperty<*>) and, for var, setValue. These can be member or extension functions, and the delegate doesn't have to implement any interface. lazy works because the stdlib has an inline extension Lazy<T>.getValue that returns value.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
source:   class C { var prop: String by MyDelegate() }

roughly:  class C {
            private val prop$delegate = MyDelegate()        // evaluated once, at construction
            var prop: String
              get()  = prop$delegate.getValue(this, C::prop)
              set(v) = prop$delegate.setValue(this, C::prop, v)
          }
  • The by expression is evaluated once, at construction, in declaration order. It is not evaluated on each access.
  • thisRef is the owning instance (or null/Nothing? for top-level and local properties). The property argument is a lightweight KProperty object, which gives you name and the return type. Using its name does not need kotlin-reflect. Calling full reflection APIs on it does.
  • Rules for signatures: getValue returns T or a subtype. setValue takes T or a supertype. thisRef must be the owner type or a supertype. All of them must be marked operator.
  • Where delegates show up in Android:
Delegate Where getValue comes from
by lazy {} stdlib Lazy<T>.getValue extension
by viewModels() ViewModelLazy implements Lazy<VM>
by navArgs() NavArgsLazy implements Lazy<Args>
by remember { mutableStateOf(0) } Compose State.getValue / MutableState.setValue extensions
by map stdlib Map.getValue extension
  • The compiler can skip the $delegate field when the delegate is a property reference, a named object, this, a constant, an enum entry or null, or a final same-module val with a default getter (per the kotlinlang delegated-properties docs). It calls the target directly instead.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Trimmed : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, String> {
    private var v = ""
    override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>) = v
    override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: String) { v = value.trim() }
}

class Form {
    var name: String by Trimmed()   // one Trimmed instance per Form instance
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking the delegate is created on each access. It is created once per owner instance.
  • Sharing a single delegate instance across many properties or owners, for example a top-level val d = Trimmed() used as by d. They then share state.
  • Assuming property.name drags in kotlin-reflect. It doesn't.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can the delegate type differ from the property type? → Yes. getValue's return type just has to be assignable to the property type.
  2. What's the memory cost? → One delegate object per owner instance per property. A lazy is roughly a 16–24 byte header-plus-fields object plus its initializer lambda. That's fine for a ViewModel, but it matters for 100k list items.
  3. Can you use delegates on extension properties? → Only delegates that don't need per-instance storage. An extension property has no field to hold x$delegate, so the delegate is effectively shared (static) state.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "by forwards to another object". The senior answer writes the desugared form, explains evaluation timing, says which delegates are Lazy underneath, and knows when the compiler elides the delegate field.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team put by observable properties on a model that was instantiated 50k times during sync. Each property added a delegate object and a lambda. The heap dump showed the delegates using more memory than the data itself.

questions.promptHtml: When can you use const val, how does it differ from a plain val or a @JvmField val in bytecode, and why does that difference matter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Constant inlining is behind a whole class of "the code changed but the app didn't" bugs. It also shows whether you know how Java callers see your declarations.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: const val is a compile-time constant. It's allowed only at top level or inside an object or companion, only for primitives and String, and only with a constant initializer and no custom getter. The compiler inlines the literal value into every call site, and it compiles to a public static final field, so it can also be used in annotations. A plain val is a private field behind a getter, read at runtime. @JvmField exposes the field directly, with no getter, but it is still read at runtime, not inlined. The trap: because const is copied into consumers, changing it in a library doesn't affect already-compiled consumers until they are recompiled.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Declaration (in companion object) Java sees Inlined into callers? Usable in annotations?
const val TIMEOUT = 30 static final int TIMEOUT = 30 on the outer class Yes, the literal 30 is copied Yes
@JvmField val TIMEOUT = 30 static final int TIMEOUT field No, read at runtime (the JVM can still treat it as constant once loaded) No
val TIMEOUT = 30 private static field plus Companion.getTIMEOUT() No No
  • Restrictions on @JvmField: the property needs a backing field and can't be private, open, override, const or delegated.
  • What "inlined" means: if (elapsed > Config.TIMEOUT) compiles to bipush 30 in the caller's class file. The caller holds no reference to Config at all for that read, which is also why reading a const doesn't trigger class initialization of its owner.
  • Inside one Gradle project, Kotlin incremental compilation tracks constant changes and recompiles dependents. Staleness appears across binary boundaries: published AARs/JARs, prebuilt SDKs, plugin or host APIs, and broken build caches (see Q181).
  • Android resource IDs are the same problem solved by tooling. Library-module R fields have long been non-final so their values aren't inlined. AGP 8.0 also made app-module R fields non-final by default (android.nonFinalResIds=true), which helps build speed and avoids stale inlined IDs. Java switch on R.id breaks under that setting, while Kotlin when still works because it doesn't need constants.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
object Api {
    const val VERSION = "v3"              // copied into callers' bytecode
    @JvmField val BASE_URL = "https://x" // a real field read
    val TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000L              // read via a getter
}

@Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME)
annotation class Endpoint(val version: String)

@Endpoint(Api.VERSION)   // OK: annotations need a compile-time constant
// @Endpoint(Api.BASE_URL) // does not compile
class SearchCall

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Exposing const val from a library for values you intend to change, like feature flags, server keys or versions. Consumers bake the old value in.
  • Using const for a "constant" that depends on BuildConfig from another module (BuildConfig fields are static final and get inlined too).
  • Expecting a const change to show up in a dependent module that was compiled from cache.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can const be a Long from a function call like TimeUnit.SECONDS.toMillis(30)? → No. The initializer must be a compile-time constant expression, such as literals and arithmetic or string concatenation on other constants.
  2. Does reading const val trigger <clinit> of the companion's outer class? → No. The value is inlined, so the class isn't touched for that read.
  3. How should a library expose a changeable value? → As a val or @JvmStatic getter, or a function. Keep const for values that must never change for the life of the ABI, or that annotations need.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "const is compile-time, so it's faster". The senior answer explains call-site inlining, the ABI and binary-compatibility consequences, the no-class-init property, and when to avoid const in a public library API.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An analytics SDK shipped const val SCHEMA_VERSION = 4. The app updated the SDK to schema 5, but a prebuilt internal AAR compiled against 4 kept sending 4, and the backend dropped events from that module for a week.

questions.promptHtml: How do top-level properties compile on the JVM, when are they initialized, and what are the thread-safety and initialization-order consequences?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Top-level vals are used as cheap singletons. Senior candidates know they are really static state with JVM class-init semantics.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A top-level property in Prefs.kt becomes a private static field of a facade class PrefsKt, with a static getter. Its initializer runs in PrefsKt's static initializer when the class is first initialized, which happens on first access to any top-level member of that file. The JVM guarantees class initialization runs exactly once and safely publishes the values, so initialization is thread-safe. Mutation afterwards isn't. Across files, a circular initialization can expose default values (null/0) even for non-null types.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
// Prefs.kt
val DEFAULT_LOCALE: Locale = Locale.getDefault()
var cachedUser: User? = null
fun foo() {}

// bytecode (simplified)
public final class PrefsKt {
  private static final Locale DEFAULT_LOCALE;   // set in <clinit>
  private static User cachedUser;
  static { DEFAULT_LOCALE = Locale.getDefault(); }
  public static Locale getDEFAULT_LOCALE() {...}
  public static void foo() {...}
}
  • Laziness is per file, not per property. Calling foo() initializes every top-level property in Prefs.kt. If one of them does disk I/O, any unrelated helper call from that file pays for it, possibly on the main thread during startup.
  • @file:JvmName("Prefs") renames the facade class. const val is inlined and doesn't trigger <clinit>.
  • Order: properties are initialized in textual order within the file. Across files, if A.kt's initializer reads B.kt's property and B.kt's initializer reads back into A.kt, one side sees a not-yet-initialized default.
  • Thread-safety: <clinit> is guarded by the JVM class-init lock, which publishes the values safely. A top-level var mutated from several threads is ordinary shared mutable state. Use atomics or confinement (see the coroutines synchronization chunk).
  • Deadlock risk: two threads initializing two classes whose <clinit>s depend on each other can deadlock on the class-init locks. The same shape as Q183, at the class level.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Risky: real I/O in a file-level initializer, paid by whoever first touches the file
val config: Config = Config.parse(File("/data/.../config.json").readText())

// Better: deferred, explicit, injectable
val configLazy: Config by lazy { Config.parse(File("/data/.../config.json").readText()) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating a top-level var as a safe global cache. It survives configuration changes, but it is wiped on process death and has no thread-safety.
  • Putting Context-dependent state at top level (lateinit var appContext), which hides dependencies and breaks tests.
  • Assuming top-level vals initialize individually when first read.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Top-level vs object property? → Both are static under the hood. An object gives you a named type, a separate class-init boundary (separate laziness) and the ability to implement interfaces.
  2. Is a top-level by lazy initialized when the file's class loads? → The Lazy object is created in <clinit>. The initializer runs on first read of that property.
  3. How do you test code that reads a top-level val? → You mostly can't swap it. That's the argument for injecting dependencies instead.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "it's like a static". The senior answer explains file-level laziness, safe publication by class init, cross-file ordering hazards and the startup-cost implication.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Utils.kt held a top-level val gson = GsonBuilder()...create() with heavy reflection registration. A trivial formatDate() call from Application.onCreate initialized it, which added about 40 ms to cold start in a Perfetto trace.

questions.promptHtml: Explain LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED, PUBLICATION and NONE: how each is implemented and when you would pick each on Android.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: by lazy is everywhere. The modes test real concurrency understanding: locks, volatile, CAS and safe publication.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: SYNCHRONIZED is the default. It uses double-checked locking with a volatile field, so the initializer runs at most once and every thread sees the same value. PUBLICATION allows several threads to run the initializer concurrently, but a compare-and-set means only the first result wins and everyone sees it. NONE has no locking and no volatile, so it's only correct if the value is created and used on a single thread. After initialization the default mode costs just one volatile read, so I use NONE for main-thread-only objects as a micro-optimisation, and I keep SYNCHRONIZED whenever more than one thread can touch the value.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mode stdlib impl Initializer runs Post-init read Use when
SYNCHRONIZED SynchronizedLazyImpl exactly once (if it succeeds) 1 volatile read default; any cross-thread access
PUBLICATION SafePublicationLazyImpl (atomic field updater CAS) possibly multiple times concurrently; first value published 1 volatile read initializer is idempotent and cheap; you want to avoid a lock (and lock-related deadlocks)
NONE UnsafeLazyImpl once if single-threaded; anything goes otherwise plain read confined to one thread (main-thread UI objects)

SynchronizedLazyImpl.value, simplified:

v1 = _value (volatile)
if v1 !== UNINITIALIZED -> return v1           // fast path, no lock
synchronized(lock) {                            // lock = this, or the one you pass via lazy(lock) { }
    v2 = _value
    if v2 !== UNINITIALIZED -> return v2
    typed = initializer!!()
    _value = typed
    initializer = null                          // releases captured references (see Q173)
    return typed
}
  • lazy(lock: Any?) { } lets you pass a custom monitor. That's useful when several lazies must share one lock, and dangerous because external code can then contend on it.
  • PUBLICATION: a losing thread's computed value is discarded. If the initializer has side effects, such as registering a listener or opening a file, those side effects happen more than once.
  • NONE used across threads can return a value whose fields another thread sees half-built (no happens-before), or run the initializer twice. That's rare in tests and real on many-core devices.
  • Android reality: most by lazy in Activities and Fragments are touched only on the main thread, so NONE is correct but saves very little. The uncontended monitor is taken once, and later reads cost a volatile read. Do it consistently, or don't bother. Correctness matters more than nanoseconds.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ProfileFragment : Fragment() {
    // main-thread only: NONE is fine
    private val dateFormat by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE) { DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("d MMM") }
}

object Crypto {
    // accessed from IO and Default dispatchers: keep the default SYNCHRONIZED
    val cipherSpec by lazy { buildSpec() }

    // idempotent and cheap, called from many threads, no lock wanted
    val pattern by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) { Regex("[a-z]+") }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using NONE in a singleton or repository that coroutines read from Dispatchers.IO or Dispatchers.Default.
  • Using PUBLICATION with a side-effecting initializer.
  • Doing blocking work inside a SYNCHRONIZED initializer that runs on main. Every other thread waits, and you get the ANR in Q183.
  • Thinking NONE is significantly faster after init. It isn't.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you check whether a lazy has been initialized without triggering it? → Keep the Lazy object (val l = lazy {}; val x by l) and call l.isInitialized().
  2. Is SYNCHRONIZED reentrant if the initializer reads the same property? → The JVM monitor is reentrant, so the same thread re-enters, still sees UNINITIALIZED, and calls the initializer again. You get infinite recursion and a StackOverflowError, not a deadlock.
  3. Is a lazy inside a coroutine-heavy class safe if the initializer suspends? → The initializer can't suspend, because the lambda isn't suspend. Calling runBlocking inside it to fake that holds the monitor while blocking, which is a deadlock and ANR recipe. Use a Deferred, or a Mutex with a nullable cache.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists the three modes. The senior answer describes the implementation (double-checked locking, CAS, initializer nulling), the real post-init cost, the side-effect implication of PUBLICATION, and the reentrancy and blocking hazards.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An image-pipeline singleton used lazy(NONE) for its disk cache. Two IO-dispatcher coroutines raced on first access, so two caches opened the same journal file and corrupted it on a small share of devices.

questions.promptHtml: What do Delegates.observable, Delegates.vetoable and Delegates.notNull do, when does each callback run, and when would you use them in an Android codebase?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These are the stdlib's ready-made delegates. Interviewers check the callback timing details and whether you know when a reactive type is the better tool.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: observable(initial) { prop, old, new -> } stores the value and calls the handler after each assignment. It fires even if the new value equals the old one. vetoable(initial) { prop, old, new -> Boolean } runs the handler before the assignment, and returning false rejects the new value. notNull() is a var that throws IllegalStateException if you read it before assigning it. Unlike lateinit, it works with primitives. I use observable for local reactions such as an adapter that refreshes when items is set, vetoable for cheap validation, and I reach for StateFlow when anyone outside the class needs to observe.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Both come from ObservableProperty<V>, which has two hooks: beforeChange(property, old, new): Boolean (default true) and afterChange(property, old, new). observable overrides afterChange. vetoable overrides beforeChange. You can subclass ObservableProperty to get both.
  • Sequence on x = v: beforeChange → if it returns true, store → afterChange. All of it runs synchronously on the calling thread. There is no locking, so two threads assigning at once can interleave the store and the callbacks.
  • No equality check: items = items triggers the handler. If you only care about real changes, add if (old != new).
  • notNull vs lateinit:
lateinit var by Delegates.notNull()
Primitives (Int, Long) Not allowed Allowed (boxed inside the delegate)
Storage backing field, null means unset delegate object
Check before use ::x.isInitialized none (you'd have to catch the exception)
Error UninitializedPropertyAccessException IllegalStateException("Property x should be initialized before get.")
Allocation none 1 delegate per property per instance

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ContactsAdapter : RecyclerView.Adapter<ContactVH>() {
    var items: List<Contact> by Delegates.observable(emptyList()) { _, old, new ->
        if (old !== new) notifyDataSetChanged() // shortcut: full refresh; use ListAdapter/DiffUtil for real lists
    }
    // ...
}

class VolumeControl {
    var level: Int by Delegates.vetoable(5) { _, _, new -> new in 0..10 } // out-of-range writes are ignored
    var sessionId: Long by Delegates.notNull()                            // must be set before first read
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Silent vetoable rejection. The caller gets no error and the value just doesn't change. That's a surprising API: throw or return a Result if callers must know.
  • Doing heavy work or posting to the UI inside observable from a background thread.
  • Using observable as the ViewModel-to-UI channel. It isn't lifecycle-aware, it doesn't replay, and it leaks if the listener captures a View.
  • Forgetting that the initial value doesn't trigger the callback.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a vetoable callback modify new (for example, clamp it)? → No, it can only accept or reject. For clamping, use a custom setter with field = v.coerceIn(0, 10).
  2. Does observable fire on construction? → No. The initial value is stored directly.
  3. Why is notNull rarely seen in modern code? → For DI you use lateinit (field injection) or constructor injection. For primitives, a nullable or default value is usually clearer than a delegate that throws.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "a callback when the value changes". The senior answer gives exact timing, says there's no equality check and no thread-safety, compares notNull with lateinit precisely, and says when to escalate to StateFlow.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom chart View used observable for data and called requestLayout(). A background loader assigned data off the main thread, so the callback ran on that thread and threw CalledFromWrongThreadException. It only reproduced when the network was slow enough for the loader to finish after the View was attached.

questions.promptHtml: How does val name: String by map work, what happens when the key is missing or the type is wrong, and where is map delegation a good or bad idea?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's a neat trick that hides runtime failure modes. Seniors know where the type safety ends.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The stdlib has getValue and setValue operator extensions on Map and MutableMap. They use property.name as the key, so val name by map is map["name"], cast to the property type. val needs a Map<String, *> and var needs a MutableMap. The map is read on every access, so it stays live, not copied. A missing key throws NoSuchElementException unless the map was wrapped with withDefault. A wrong value type fails with a ClassCastException at the point of access, not at construction. That makes it fine for loosely typed, already-validated data like remote config or test fixtures, and bad for core domain models.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Lookup goes through getOrImplicitDefault(property.name), so map.withDefault { key -> ... } is honoured by the delegate (but not by plain map[key]).
  • The cast is unchecked, so failures appear late:
Map content for key "age" Property val age: Int by map
missing NoSuchElementException: Key age is missing in the map.
"42" (String) ClassCastException when age is read
null an NPE-style failure at the use site for a non-null type. Declare Int? if null is legal.
42.0 (Double, typical from a JSON parser) ClassCastException. JSON numbers often come back as Double/Long.
  • Renaming the property with an IDE refactor silently changes the key. R8 obfuscation does not change it: the name comes from compiler-generated metadata strings, not from the obfuscated member name. Still verify in a release build, because this is easy to get wrong.
  • With var and MutableMap, writes go into the map, which is useful for "dirty field" style forms that you serialise back as a map.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class RemoteFlags(raw: Map<String, Any?>) {
    private val m = raw.withDefault { key -> DEFAULTS[key] }
    val newCheckout: Boolean by m
    val maxRetries: Long by m           // JSON numbers parsed as Long: match the parser's types
    companion object { val DEFAULTS = mapOf("newCheckout" to false, "maxRetries" to 3L) }
}

class Draft(val fields: MutableMap<String, Any?> = mutableMapOf()) {
    var title: String? by fields       // writes land in the map, ready to send as a PATCH
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using it with parsed JSON and getting Double where you expected Int.
  • Keeping a reference to a mutable source map and being surprised that property values change under you.
  • Rename refactors that change the wire key.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is the map copied? → No. The delegate is the map reference itself, so each read is a hash lookup.
  2. Does withDefault affect map["x"]? → No, only getValue and the delegate. map["x"] still returns null.
  3. How would you make this type-safe? → Parse once into a data class with kotlinx.serialization (or Moshi) at the boundary, and validate there. Map delegation only moves the failure to the time of access.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "property name = key". The senior answer explains that reads are live, withDefault, late ClassCastException with JSON number types, rename hazards, and when to parse into a typed model instead.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Remote-config flags delegated by map read maxRetries as Int, but the config SDK returned Long. Every access to the retry path crashed with a ClassCastException, and only the first user session after a config fetch hit it.

questions.promptHtml: What does class LoggingRepo(private val inner: Repo) : Repo by inner generate, and why is it the idiomatic way to build decorators in Kotlin?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests composition over inheritance, the decorator pattern and how the compiler saves you boilerplate. Most real-world uses on Android are decorators.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Class delegation implements an interface by forwarding every member you don't override to the object after by. The compiler generates the forwarding methods and keeps the delegate in a hidden field. You override only what you want to change, like logging, caching or metrics, and the rest passes through. It works only for interfaces, not classes, and it gives you the decorator pattern without writing 30 one-line forwarders or inheriting from a concrete class.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
interface Repo { fun get(id: String): Item; fun all(): List<Item>; fun save(i: Item) }

class LoggingRepo(private val inner: Repo) : Repo by inner {
    override fun save(i: Item) { log("save ${i.id}"); inner.save(i) }
}

// generated (roughly)
class LoggingRepo(inner: Repo) : Repo {
    private final Repo $$delegate_0 = inner;            // evaluated once
    fun get(id) = $$delegate_0.get(id)                   // generated forwarder
    fun all()   = $$delegate_0.all()                     // generated forwarder
    override fun save(i) { log(...); inner.save(i) }     // yours
}
  • The expression after by is evaluated once at construction and stored. If you delegate to a constructor var and reassign it later, delegation keeps using the original object.
  • You can delegate several interfaces: class X(a: A, b: B) : A by a, B by b. If two interfaces declare the same member, you must override it.
  • Why not inheritance: subclassing a concrete RepoImpl couples you to its constructor, its internal calls and its future changes (the fragile base class problem). Delegation depends only on the interface contract.
  • Android uses: wrapping Repo with a cache or metrics layer, test fakes that forward to a real impl and override one method, MutableList<T> by backing to add invariants, and CoroutineScope by MainScope() in older code (see the coroutines chunks for why that style is discouraged now).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class CountingList<T>(private val inner: MutableList<T> = ArrayList()) : MutableList<T> by inner {
    var adds = 0; private set
    override fun add(element: T): Boolean { adds++; return inner.add(element) }
    override fun addAll(elements: Collection<T>): Boolean { adds += elements.size; return inner.addAll(elements) }
    // add(index, element) still forwards with no count -> every overload must be overridden
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Overriding one overload (add(e)) and forgetting the others (add(i, e), addAll), so the invariant leaks.
  • Calling this.save() from inside a delegate method and expecting your override to run. It won't (see Q174).
