  • Delegating to a class type. That's not allowed, only interfaces.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Are equals, hashCode and toString delegated? → No. Members of Any aren't forwarded, so the wrapper uses its own identity unless you override them.
  2. Can I reach the delegate field from outside? → Only if you also declare it as a property (private val inner). The synthetic field isn't accessible.
  3. What happens when the interface gains a new method? → The compiler silently forwards it. That's convenient, and for decorators that must intercept every write it's also a hazard (see Q184).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "by avoids boilerplate". The senior answer explains evaluation-once semantics, that Any members aren't delegated, overload completeness, and why delegation beats inheriting from concrete classes for decorators.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A CachingUserRepo : UserRepo by remote overrode getUser but not getUsers(ids). The batch screen bypassed the cache completely and tripled backend QPS after a feature launch.

questions.promptHtml: Write a custom property delegate, for example a Fragment-argument delegate, and explain the type parameters of ReadWriteProperty<T, V> and the design choices you made.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Building a delegate shows you understand thisRef, KProperty, variance and where state lives. Interviewers often ask for it live.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ReadOnlyProperty<in T, out V> has getValue(thisRef: T, property: KProperty<*>): V. ReadWriteProperty<in T, V> adds setValue. T is the owner type: the delegate can only be used inside classes of that type, and it gets the instance through thisRef. V is the value type. For a Fragment argument delegate, T is Fragment, the key is property.name, and the value lives in arguments, not in the delegate. That matters because the Bundle is saved and restored across process death, while a field in the delegate would not be.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Variance: T is in because a delegate that accepts any Fragment can be used inside a ProfileFragment. In ReadOnlyProperty, V is out. In ReadWriteProperty, V is invariant because it is both read and written.
  • Where state lives is the key design question:
Store state in... Survives config change Survives process death Example
the delegate's own field no (the new Fragment gets a new delegate) no memo caches
thisRef.arguments (Bundle) yes yes screen inputs
SavedStateHandle yes (VM) yes ViewModel state
SharedPreferences/DataStore yes yes, but it's disk I/O (Q180) settings
  • Pass a key explicitly, or default to property.name. Using the name couples persisted keys to property names, so a rename breaks restoring old Bundles and prefs.
  • The stdlib also has fun interface-style factories: ReadOnlyProperty { thisRef, property -> ... } is a SAM-convertible lambda (since Kotlin 1.4), which works for quick read-only delegates.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun stringArg(key: String? = null): ReadWriteProperty<Fragment, String> =
    object : ReadWriteProperty<Fragment, String> {
        override fun getValue(thisRef: Fragment, property: KProperty<*>): String =
            thisRef.requireArguments().getString(key ?: property.name)
                ?: error("Missing argument '${key ?: property.name}' for ${thisRef::class.simpleName}")

        override fun setValue(thisRef: Fragment, property: KProperty<*>, value: String) {
            val args = thisRef.arguments ?: Bundle().also { thisRef.arguments = it }
            args.putString(key ?: property.name, value)
        }
    }

class ProfileFragment : Fragment() {
    var userId: String by stringArg("user_id")   // stable key, safe to rename the property
    companion object { fun newInstance(id: String) = ProfileFragment().apply { userId = id } }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Caching the value in the delegate. It becomes stale if arguments change, and it's lost on recreation.
  • Calling setArguments after the Fragment is added. That throws IllegalStateException once the state is saved.
  • Making a generic arg<T>() with bundle.get(key) as T. That's an unchecked cast and a deprecated API on API 33+. Prefer typed variants or BundleCompat.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does ReadWriteProperty extend ReadOnlyProperty? → So a read-write delegate can be passed anywhere a read-only one is expected. That also lets you put a val on a read-write delegate.
  2. Can a delegate be object-shared across instances? → Yes, if it is stateless and gets everything from thisRef, as above. Named object delegates also skip the $delegate field.
  3. How would you make this work for val only, with a lambda? → fun intArg(k: String) = ReadOnlyProperty<Fragment, Int> { f, _ -> f.requireArguments().getInt(k) }.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer writes a delegate that holds a field. The senior answer starts from where state must survive (configuration change and process death), explains variance on T and V, and avoids name-coupled keys.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team-built by argument() delegate cached the value in a field. After process death, the restored Fragment read the field (empty) instead of the restored Bundle and showed a blank profile, about 0.3% of sessions on low-RAM devices.

questions.subtopic: Android delegates: viewModels, activityViewModels, navGraphViewModels, navArgs
questions.promptHtml: What do by viewModels(), by activityViewModels(), by navGraphViewModels() and by navArgs() actually return, when is it legal to access them, and how do you choose the ViewModel scope?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These four lines appear in almost every Fragment. Seniors know they're just Lazy objects with owner rules, and that the wrong scope causes state bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: All four are Lazy implementations. viewModels and activityViewModels return a ViewModelLazy that, on first access, asks a ViewModelProvider for the VM using an owner's ViewModelStore. That owner is the Fragment, the Activity (requireActivity()) or a NavBackStackEntry for a nav graph. navArgs returns NavArgsLazy, which reads arguments and calls the generated Safe Args fromBundle. Declaring them is free, but the first access must happen while the Fragment is attached, normally from onCreate/onViewCreated onwards. Access too early or after detach and you get an IllegalStateException. Scope means lifetime: the Fragment for screen state, the nav graph for a multi-screen flow, the Activity only for state that truly spans the whole Activity.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Delegate Owner (ViewModelStoreOwner) VM cleared when Throws if accessed
viewModels() this Fragment Fragment is removed for good (not on config change) before attach / after destroy: "Can't access ViewModels from detached fragment"
viewModels(ownerProducer = { requireParentFragment() }) parent Fragment parent removed parent not available
activityViewModels() host Activity Activity finishes before attach: "Fragment ... not attached to an activity"
navGraphViewModels(R.id.checkout) / hiltNavGraphViewModels(R.id.checkout) graph's NavBackStackEntry graph popped off the back stack graph not on the back stack
navArgs() n/a, reads arguments n/a arguments null: "Fragment ... has null arguments"
  • ViewModelLazy.value: if a VM is cached in the lazy, return it. Otherwise call ViewModelProvider(store, factory, extras)[VM::class]. The store keeps the VM across configuration changes. The lazy itself is per Fragment instance and is recreated with the Fragment.
  • Factories and extras: the default factory uses defaultViewModelProviderFactory (Hilt replaces it) and CreationExtras, which supply SavedStateHandle from the owner's saved state.
  • NavArgsLazy caches args after the first read. Safe Args fromBundle is called through reflection, so its keep rules are needed (the navigation artifacts ship them).
  • by viewModels is just Lazy, so ::vm.isInitialized isn't available. If you need to check, keep the Lazy object.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@AndroidEntryPoint
class PaymentFragment : Fragment(R.layout.payment) {
    private val vm: PaymentViewModel by viewModels()                        // this screen only
    private val flow: CheckoutViewModel by hiltNavGraphViewModels(R.id.checkout_graph) // the whole flow
    private val args: PaymentFragmentArgs by navArgs()

    // BROKEN: field initializer runs at construction, before attach -> IllegalStateException
    // private val orderId = args.orderId

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        vm.load(args.orderId) // OK: attached
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading a delegate in a property initializer or init block, which runs at construction time.
  • Reading by viewModels() from a callback that fires after onDestroy (Q179).
  • activityViewModels as a convenient global bus, so state outlives the flow it belongs to (Q185).
  • Passing navArgs into the VM manually instead of reading SavedStateHandle in the VM, which duplicates the source of truth.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does the VM get the nav args without the Fragment? → The SavedStateHandle from the default CreationExtras is seeded with the Fragment's arguments, so savedStateHandle.get<String>("orderId") works, or SavedStateHandle.toRoute<T>() with type-safe navigation in Navigation 2.8+.
  2. Two Fragments both use activityViewModels<SharedVm>(). Same instance? → Yes, same store and same key (class name), so it's one instance.
  3. What's the Compose equivalent? → viewModel() / hiltViewModel() in a composable, scoped to the nearest LocalViewModelStoreOwner (a nav back stack entry under Navigation Compose).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "viewModels survives rotation". The senior answer explains Lazy and store mechanics, when access is legal, the exact exceptions, scope-as-lifetime reasoning, and SavedStateHandle as the route for args.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Fragment read activityViewModels() from a property initializer. It worked in normal navigation, because the Fragment was attached quickly. It crashed with "not attached to an activity" when restored by FragmentManager in an unusual order after process death.

questions.promptHtml: What happens if a lazy initializer throws? What does a Lazy keep alive in memory before and after initialization, and how can by lazy cause a leak?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The behaviour on failure and the retention of captured references are the parts of lazy people never look at, and they're behind real crashes and leaks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If the initializer throws, nothing is cached. The exception propagates, and the next access runs the initializer again. That is good for transient failures but bad when the initializer is expensive or has side effects, because you get retry storms. Before initialization, the Lazy holds the initializer lambda and everything it captured. The stdlib sets the initializer to null after success, so captured objects are released. The value itself is held as long as the Lazy is, which means as long as its owner. So by lazy leaks when a long-lived owner (a singleton or a top-level property) caches something that holds an Activity, Fragment or View, or when it's never initialized and keeps the captured lambda forever.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Lazy states (SynchronizedLazyImpl)

  [UNINIT] initializer = lambda(+captures)  _value = UNINITIALIZED
     | first get()
     |-- initializer throws --> stays UNINIT, exception rethrown to the caller
     |                          (each later get() retries)
     '-- returns v ----------> [INIT] initializer = null   _value = v (held until the owner is GC'd)
  • Retention matrix:
Owner lifetime Lazy captures / caches Result
object/singleton/top-level activity captured in the lambda, never read Activity leaked until first read (maybe forever)
singleton value built from activity (e.g. a LayoutInflater or a themed Context) Activity leaked for the process lifetime
Fragment a View (by lazy { view.findViewById() }) stale View after onDestroyView (Q178)
ViewModel applicationContext fine
  • Exceptions are not cached. A lazy { Database.open(path) } that fails because the disk is full will be retried on every access. Each try costs IO, and with a SYNCHRONIZED lock, every thread queues behind it. If you need "fail once, then degrade", cache a Result instead: lazy { runCatching { open() } }, and decide your policy at the call site. Be careful that runCatching also catches CancellationException if the code runs inside a coroutine (see the cancellation chunk).
  • Lazy is Serializable. On serialisation it writes the computed value, which forces initialization. That rarely matters on Android, but it's a surprise in Bundles holding Serializable objects.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// LEAK: the singleton outlives the Activity; the cached value holds the Activity context
object ImageLoaderHolder {
    lateinit var ctx: Context
    val loader by lazy { ImageLoader(ctx) } // if ctx is an Activity, it's pinned forever
}

// FIX: capture only the application context
class AppImageLoader @Inject constructor(@ApplicationContext private val app: Context) {
    val loader by lazy { ImageLoader(app) }
}

// Cache failure explicitly, so you don't retry an expensive open on every read
val dbResult: Result<Db> by lazy { runCatching { Db.open(file) } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming an initializer exception is cached like a value.
  • by lazy in a companion object that captures an instance's members. Companion lazies are static state.
  • Thinking lazy holds its value weakly. It holds it strongly.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is the initializer nulled in PUBLICATION and NONE too? → Yes. All three stdlib implementations drop the initializer reference after a successful initialization.
  2. How would you build a lazy that can be reset, for example when the user logs out? → lazy can't be reset. Use a nullable field guarded by a lock or Mutex, or scope the object to a DI component (a user session scope) that is thrown away.
  3. LeakCanary shows SynchronizedLazyImpl._value → ContextThemeWrapper → MainActivity. What's the fix? → Find the long-lived owner holding that lazy, then either make the cached value application-scoped or move the lazy to an owner whose lifetime matches the Activity.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "lazy initializes once". The senior answer covers non-caching of failures, initializer release, strong retention tied to owner lifetime, and the reset/scoping alternatives.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A lazy { remoteConfig.fetchBlocking() } threw on every access during an outage. Every screen that read it retried a 10 s network timeout under the lazy's lock, which caused a wave of ANRs, all from one property.

questions.promptHtml: With class delegation, if the delegate calls one of its own methods internally, does the wrapper's override run? What else does by not do that inheritance would?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This is the "self problem" of delegation vs inheritance. It separates people who use by from people who understand it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: No. Delegation is forwarding, not inheritance. When inner.addAll() internally calls this.add(), this is the inner object, so your wrapper's add override never runs. Only callers that go through the wrapper see the overrides. Also, by forwards only interface members. It doesn't forward Any members (equals/hashCode/toString), it can't reach protected or non-interface members of the delegate, and it binds the delegate once at construction. If your design depends on the inner object calling back into the wrapper, you need inheritance or an explicit callback, not by.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
caller ---> Wrapper.addAll()  (not overridden -> forwarded)
                 |
                 v
            inner.addAll()  -- calls this.add() --> inner.add()   (Wrapper.add NOT called)

With inheritance (class Wrapper : ArrayList()):
caller ---> Wrapper.addAll() -> super.addAll() -> this.add() --> Wrapper.add()  (virtual dispatch)
  • Which is "right" depends on the case. Inheritance's virtual self-call is exactly what makes subclassing fragile: whether ArrayList.addAll calls add is an implementation detail that can change. Delegation makes behaviour predictable, at the price of overriding every entry point you care about.
  • Other limits:
    • Only interfaces. You can't do : SomeClass by x.
    • Bound once. class W(var d: Repo) : Repo by d: reassigning d doesn't change who receives the forwarded calls. They still go to the original object stored in the synthetic field.
    • Generated forwarders are real methods. Java and Kotlin callers see them, and stack traces show the wrapper frame.
    • Default methods. For Kotlin interfaces with default bodies, the wrapper forwards to the delegate's implementation, not the interface default. For Java default methods and -Xjvm-default modes the exact codegen depends on compiler settings, so check the bytecode if it matters.
    • Delegate to this? Not possible: the expression is evaluated before the instance is fully constructed and can't refer to it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface Sink { fun write(s: String); fun writeAll(xs: List<String>) = xs.forEach { write(it) } }

class FileSink : Sink { override fun write(s: String) { /* disk */ } }

class RedactingSink(private val inner: Sink) : Sink by inner {
    override fun write(s: String) = inner.write(s.replace(Regex("\\d{16}"), "****"))
}

fun main() {
    val sink = RedactingSink(FileSink())
    sink.write("card 4111111111111111")          // redacted
    sink.writeAll(listOf("card 4111111111111111")) // NOT redacted: forwarded to inner.writeAll,
                                                   // which calls inner.write
}
// Fix: override writeAll too, or move the policy into a single entry point the delegate can't bypass.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming template-method-style hooks still work through by.
  • Decorating a security or privacy policy (redaction, auth) with by and missing one entry point.
  • Expecting toString() on the wrapper to show the inner object's state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you get both: forwarding by default plus callbacks? → Design the interface so the delegate receives the wrapper explicitly (a strategy or listener parameter), or use inheritance from an abstract class you own and designed for extension.
  2. Does delegation cost performance? → One extra virtual call per forwarded method, which is usually negligible. ART can inline monomorphic call sites.
  3. How do you catch a missed entry point in review? → Keep the wrapped interface small. Add a test that drives every interface method through the wrapper (reflection over Sink::class.members), or prefer an explicit wrapper where the compiler forces you to implement everything.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "you override what you need". The senior answer explains forwarding vs virtual self-call, why it's both safer and riskier than inheritance, bind-once, non-forwarded Any members, and how to design interfaces so decorators can't be bypassed.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A PII-redacting logger wrapped the logging interface with by. Batch logging (logAll) went through the delegate's own default method straight to the inner log, and raw emails reached the log backend until an audit found them.

questions.promptHtml: What is provideDelegate, when is it called relative to getValue, and what real problem does it solve that a plain delegate can't?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This is the advanced corner of delegation, used by Gradle's Kotlin DSL, binding libraries and registries. It shows whether you can design delegate-based APIs, not just consume them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If the object after by has an operator fun provideDelegate(thisRef, property), the compiler calls it once per property, when the owner is being constructed, and stores whatever it returns as the real delegate. getValue and setValue are then called on that returned object. This gives you a hook at declaration time with the property's name and type in hand, so you can validate (duplicate keys, wrong types), register the property in a schema, or pick a delegate implementation. A plain delegate only finds out about the property on first access. The stdlib's PropertyDelegateProvider fun interface lets you write a provider as a lambda.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
class Settings { val theme by stringPref("theme") }

construction:
  provider = stringPref("theme")                    // the 'by' expression
  theme$delegate = provider.provideDelegate(this, Settings::theme)   // once, eagerly
access:
  theme$delegate.getValue(this, Settings::theme)    // every read
  • Timing: provideDelegate runs as part of the owner's initialization, in property declaration order, so it can fail fast. A bad declaration crashes at construction, which is easy to catch in a unit test, not on the first rare read in production.
  • Signatures follow getValue's rules: thisRef is the owner type or a supertype, and property is a KProperty<*>. It can be a member or an extension, so you can add provideDelegate to an existing type.
  • Typical uses:
Use What happens in provideDelegate
Schema registry (prefs keys, analytics params) add property.name / key to a set, throw on duplicates
Gradle Kotlin DSL val main by sourceSets.getting / by registering look up or register by property name
Binding libraries resolve a view or resource id once, return a cached delegate
Choosing an implementation e.g., return an encrypted delegate if the property has an annotation (needs kotlin-reflect for annotations)
  • It only changes how the $delegate field is created. The getter and setter code is the same as for any delegate.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class PrefsSchema {
    private val keys = mutableSetOf<String>()

    fun string(key: String? = null, default: String = "") =
        PropertyDelegateProvider<Any?, ReadOnlyProperty<Any?, String>> { _, prop ->
            val k = key ?: prop.name
            check(keys.add(k)) { "Duplicate pref key '$k' (property ${prop.name})" } // fails at construction
            ReadOnlyProperty { _, _ -> store.getString(k, default) }
        }

    private val store = InMemoryStore()
}

class AppPrefs(schema: PrefsSchema) {
    val theme by schema.string("theme")
    val locale by schema.string("theme") // IllegalStateException when AppPrefs is constructed
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing expensive work in provideDelegate. It runs for every owner construction, which for a Fragment means every recreation.
  • Relying on property.annotations without realising that needs full kotlin-reflect (and R8 keep rules).
  • Confusing it with lazy initialization. provideDelegate is eager.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does provideDelegate work for local delegated properties? → Yes. thisRef is null (type Nothing?), so a provider used there must accept a nullable owner.
  2. How does Gradle's val main by sourceSets.getting know the name main? → Through provideDelegate/getValue receiving property.name, which the DSL uses as the lookup key.
  3. How would you unit-test duplicate-key detection? → Construct the owner in a JVM test and assert it throws. Because the check is eager, constructing it is enough.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer has rarely heard of it. The senior answer explains eager timing, uses it for fail-fast schema validation and registration, recognises it in Gradle DSL, and knows the reflection cost of annotation-driven variants.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Two features declared the same SharedPreferences key under different property names and silently overwrote each other's settings. A provideDelegate-based schema turned that into a crash in a unit test on the next PR.

questions.subtopic: Delegating to another property, local delegates, delegation cost
questions.promptHtml: Explain var old by this::new, local delegated properties such as val x by lazy {} inside a function, and the runtime cost of delegation (objects, reflection, bytecode).

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior candidates are expected to know the cost model of what they use, and the newer delegation forms used for API evolution.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Since Kotlin 1.4 a property can delegate to another property via a reference: by this::new, by ::topLevel or by other::prop. The compiler then calls the target's accessors directly, without a delegate object. This is the clean way to rename a public property: keep the old name @Deprecated and delegate it to the new one. Local delegated properties (since 1.1) let you write val token by lazy { ... } inside a function, so it's computed only if a branch actually reads it. Costs: each ordinary delegated property means one delegate object per owner instance, plus a forwarding call per access. The class also gets static, lightweight KProperty objects. These don't need kotlin-reflect, but they are extra metadata and allocations at class init.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Property-reference delegation:
class User(var displayName: String) {
    @Deprecated("Use displayName", ReplaceWith("displayName"))
    var name: String by this::displayName   // no name$delegate field; accessors call displayName directly
}

Kotlin docs say a getName$delegate()-style method may still be generated, for reflection only.

  • Local delegated property:
fun render(user: User?, verbose: Boolean) {
    val details by lazy { expensiveDetails(user) }    // never computed if no branch reads it
    if (verbose && user != null) println(details)
    if (user?.isAdmin == true) audit(details)          // computed at most once even if both branches run
}

Note that a local lazy defaults to SYNCHRONIZED even though it's local. A lambda can leak it to another thread, so the compiler doesn't assume it's single-threaded.

  • Cost model per delegated property:
Item Allocated When
Delegate object (Lazy, ObservableProperty, custom) per owner instance owner construction
Initializer/handler lambda per owner instance if it captures; a singleton if it doesn't owner construction
KProperty reference objects per class (a static array, often named $$delegatedProperties) class init
Accessor call per access, plus the delegate's own work (e.g., a volatile read for lazy) runtime

The compiler can skip the delegate field for property references, named objects, this, constants, enum entries, null and final same-module vals with default getters. For an inline getValue that doesn't use the property argument, newer compilers can avoid touching the KProperty. This is version-dependent, so check the decompiled bytecode (Tools → Kotlin → Show Kotlin Bytecode → Decompile) before relying on it.

  • Rule of thumb: delegation costs nothing that matters in Activities, Fragments, ViewModels and singletons. It does matter in classes instantiated in the tens of thousands (list item models, parsed DTOs) or on per-frame paths.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// DTO created 50k times during sync: each 'by' adds an object + lambda per instance
class RowDto(json: JsonObject) {
    val title: String by lazy { json["t"]!!.jsonPrimitive.content }   // avoid on hot DTOs
}
// Prefer eager parsing into plain vals for hot data classes
data class Row(val title: String)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Renaming a public property and breaking binary compatibility, when @Deprecated with by this::new would have kept old callers working.
  • Putting by lazy/by observable on high-cardinality models.
  • Assuming KProperty means full reflection and adding kotlin-reflect "to be safe", which adds about 2 MB+ before R8 shrinking.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you delegate a var to a val reference? → No. The target must be mutable (KMutableProperty) for a var delegate.
  2. Is a local by lazy captured by a lambda thread-safe? → With the default SYNCHRONIZED, yes. If you choose NONE, it's your responsibility.
  3. How do you measure whether delegates matter in your hot path? → An Android Studio memory profiler allocation recording (or a heap dump: count SynchronizedLazyImpl instances), plus a Macrobenchmark or Microbenchmark of the construction path.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer knows by lazy. The senior answer uses property-reference delegation for API evolution, uses local delegates for conditional computation, and can state per-instance vs per-class costs and when the compiler elides them.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A sync parser wrapped every DTO field in by lazy "for speed". The heap dump showed about 600k SynchronizedLazyImpl and lambda objects for 50k rows. Eager parsing cut sync GC pauses by more than half.

questions.contextHtml:
A new filter screen never updates. QA: "Tap a chip, nothing changes; rotate the device and it shows the default filter." No crashes, and logs show onFilterSelected being called. 5% of the team's screens use this ViewModel template.

class FilterViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _filter get() = MutableStateFlow(Filter.ALL)
    val filter: StateFlow<Filter> get() = _filter

    fun onFilterSelected(f: Filter) {
        Log.d("Filter", "selected $f")
        _filter.value = f
    }
}

// Fragment
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        vm.filter.collect { chips.check(it.chipId) }
    }
}

A reviewer suspects repeatOnLifecycle or a missing distinctUntilChanged.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain why the symptoms look exactly like this, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "StateFlow doesn't emit equal values, so add a SharedFlow", or "collect on Main.immediate". Both chase the red herrings. They don't notice that get() builds a new object on every access, because they read val ... get() = as a field.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is _filter used anywhere else? (no) Does the collector receive the initial ALL? (yes, once) Do any other screens copy this template? (5%, so this is a sweep, not a one-off.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an outage. Fix the template, grep for MutableStateFlow( inside get() and for get() = Mutable, and patch every copy.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the custom getter creates a new MutableStateFlow per access, so the writer and the collector hold different objects. (b) Collector lifecycle wrong: no, the initial value arrives. (c) Equality conflation: only if f == ALL, but QA tapped other chips.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log System.identityHashCode(_filter) in onFilterSelected and at collect time. The IDs differ. Or decompile: get_filter() contains new MutableStateFlow(...) with no field. A unit test using Turbine: vm.filter.test { vm.onFilterSelected(RECENT); awaitItem(); awaitItem() } times out on the second item.
  5. Root cause: val x get() = expr has no backing field and evaluates expr on every read. filter reads _filter once, when the collector starts, and gets flow #1. onFilterSelected reads _filter again, gets a brand-new flow #2, and sets its value, but nobody collects #2, and it is garbage-collected right away. On rotation the collector restarts and reads _filter again, getting flow #3 with ALL. That's exactly the symptom "it shows the default after rotation".
  6. Fix: Short term: use an initializer, so there is one instance stored in a field.
class FilterViewModel(private val handle: SavedStateHandle) : ViewModel() {
    private val _filter = MutableStateFlow(Filter.ALL)
    val filter: StateFlow<Filter> = _filter.asStateFlow()
    fun onFilterSelected(f: Filter) { _filter.value = f }
}

Long term: keep filters in handle.getStateFlow("filter", Filter.ALL) so they survive process death too, and fix the template generator. 7. Prevention: A custom lint or detekt rule that flags a custom getter returning a constructor call of Mutable*Flow, MutableLiveData or mutableStateOf. A test in the template that asserts a second emission. A review checklist item: "get() = means recomputed every time". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't swap to SharedFlow or add distinctUntilChanged. That treats a symptom that doesn't exist and adds event-loss risk. I wouldn't use by lazy either: it works, but it hides intent and adds a lock for no reason.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if filter were get() = _filter.asStateFlow() with a correct _filter field? → Correct behaviour, but it allocates a wrapper per read. Harmless here, but === checks fail. Prefer assigning once.
  • Would Compose's collectAsStateWithLifecycle() hide or reveal it? → Same bug. Recomposition may even call vm.filter again and get yet another flow, which makes it worse.
  • Why doesn't the compiler warn? → val with a getter returning a new object is legal and sometimes intentional (a fresh copy). Only a custom rule knows your intent.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A copy-pasted ViewModel template with get() = MutableStateFlow(...) spread to a dozen screens before anyone noticed. Most of those screens only ever showed their initial state. A 10-line detekt rule found every instance in one CI run.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames StateFlow conflation or lifecycle and never spots the getter.
  • Hire: identifies the per-access allocation and fixes it with an initializer.
  • Strong hire: explains the rotation symptom mechanically, proves it with identity hashes or a test, adds SavedStateHandle, and proposes a lint rule plus a template fix.

questions.contextHtml:
Crash-free sessions dropped from 99.7% to 99.5% after a refactor that "removed findViewById boilerplate". The top crash is not a crash at all: users report the order list going blank after they return from the details screen. LeakCanary in debug shows OrdersFragment → ordersList$delegate → SynchronizedLazyImpl._value → RecyclerView (detached). A crash in the same release is unrelated: NullPointerException in a third-party chat SDK. That's the red herring.

class OrdersFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_orders) {
    private val ordersList by lazy { requireView().findViewById<RecyclerView>(R.id.orders) }
    private val adapter = OrdersAdapter()

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        ordersList.adapter = adapter
        viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
            viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
                vm.orders.collect { adapter.submitList(it) }
            }
        }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: What's wrong, why does it show only after going back, and how do you fix it properly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Re-submit the list in onResume", or "the adapter is cleared, use notifyDataSetChanged". It doesn't recognise that a Fragment's view lifecycle is shorter than the Fragment's lifecycle, or that lazy caches forever.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the details screen a replace with addToBackStack? (yes, so the Fragment instance stays alive and its view is destroyed) Does it reproduce with "Don't keep activities"? (that's a different path: new instance, so no bug) Are other Fragments using the same pattern? Grep by lazy { requireView() / view?.findViewById / binding inside lazy.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the delegate in the affected Fragments. It's a small diff and low risk.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) lazy caches the first view hierarchy's RecyclerView, so after onDestroyView → onCreateView the code binds the adapter to the old, detached RecyclerView. (b) Adapter state lost: unlikely, since the adapter is a field and keeps its list. (c) The collector stopped: no, repeatOnLifecycle on viewLifecycleOwner restarts with the new view.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log identityHashCode(ordersList) vs identityHashCode(view.findViewById(R.id.orders)) in the second onViewCreated. They differ. Layout Inspector shows the visible RecyclerView with no adapter. The LeakCanary trace above shows the old view retained.
  5. Root cause: On back stack navigation, a Fragment goes through onDestroyView but not onDestroy. It then gets a new view in onCreateView. The lazy belongs to the Fragment instance, not the view, so after the first initialization it always returns the first RecyclerView. ordersList.adapter = adapter attaches the adapter to the detached view, so the visible list is empty. The old view tree is also retained through _value as long as the Fragment lives, which is the leak.
  6. Fix: Short term: look the view up per view lifecycle.
class OrdersFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_orders) {
    private var _binding: FragmentOrdersBinding? = null
    private val binding get() = _binding!!          // valid only between onViewCreated and onDestroyView

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        _binding = FragmentOrdersBinding.bind(view)
        binding.orders.adapter = adapter
        // collect as before
    }
    override fun onDestroyView() {
        binding.orders.adapter = null   // the adapter outlives the view: drop the RecyclerView reference it holds
        _binding = null
        super.onDestroyView()
    }
}

Long term: one shared view-lifecycle-aware binding delegate (it clears itself on viewLifecycleOwner ON_DESTROY), or move the screen to Compose, where this class of bug doesn't exist. 7. Prevention: A lint rule that bans lazy whose initializer references requireView(), view or binding inside a Fragment. Test with a back-stack round trip (Espresso: navigate forward, press back, assert the list is displayed). Run LeakCanary in debug and on CI instrumentation. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't "fix" it by calling submitList again in onResume, which hides the stale reference and keeps the leak. I wouldn't use lazy(NONE) either: the mode is irrelevant, because the caching itself is the bug.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is by lazy { requireContext() } in a Fragment also a bug? → Less severe. It's the same Activity context until the Activity is recreated, and the Fragment is recreated with it. It is still pointless; just call requireContext().
  • Why is the adapter as a Fragment field OK? → It holds data, not views, but the RecyclerView holds the adapter and the adapter holds observers back to the RecyclerView. That's why I null adapter in onDestroyView.
  • What about by viewModels()? That's lazy too. → Yes, but it caches a ViewModel whose lifetime is at least the Fragment's. Laziness is fine when the cached object outlives the owner, and wrong when it's shorter-lived (like a view).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "Kotlin cleanup" PR converted 30 Fragments to by lazy view lookups. Every one broke only on back navigation, which no automated test covered. The fix was a single binding delegate plus one back-stack UI test per screen.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the adapter or the data and suggests re-submitting.
  • Hire: identifies the view lifecycle vs Fragment lifecycle mismatch and the lazy cache.
  • Strong hire: also explains the leak, nulls the adapter in onDestroyView, proposes a lint rule and a back-stack test, and states the general "lazy only for objects at least as long-lived as the owner" principle.

questions.subtopic: Android delegates accessed outside attach window
questions.contextHtml:
Release 6.4 (2.8M DAU). Crashlytics shows a new top crash, about 1,100 events per day, 0.04% of sessions, 70% on Android 10–12 low-end devices:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Can't access ViewModels from detached fragment
    at androidx.fragment.app.Fragment.getViewModelStore(Fragment.java:...)
    at androidx.lifecycle.ViewModelLazy.getValue(ViewModelProvider.kt:...)
    at com.app.checkout.CouponFragment.getVm(CouponFragment.kt:31)
    at com.app.checkout.CouponFragment.onCouponTimeout$lambda$3(CouponFragment.kt:88)
    at android.os.Handler.handleCallback(Handler.java:...)

The change in 6.4: the coupon screen now calls view.postDelayed({ vm.expireCoupon() }, 3_000) after showing a toast, and the vm delegate's first access moved from onViewCreated into that callback. Hilt was also upgraded in 6.4 (red herring).
questions.promptHtml: Explain the crash mechanically and fix it so that it can't recur in this form.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap it in if (isAdded)", or "roll back the Hilt upgrade". The first is a band-aid that keeps the timing hazard. The second chases the coincidence.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the crash need the user to leave within 3 s? (check breadcrumbs: back press within 3 s, yes) Why low-end devices? (slower devices finish the toast animation later, and those users tap back more often) Was vm touched anywhere before the callback? (no, so the lazy is uninitialized when the Fragment is destroyed.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remote-config off the coupon expiry auto-timer (the flag exists). Ship a hotfix that removes the delayed callback.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A delayed Runnable outlives the Fragment, and the first access to by viewModels() happens after onDestroy, when mFragmentManager is null, so getViewModelStore throws. (b) Hilt factory problem: no, the message comes from the Fragment, not the factory. (c) Process death restore: no, the stack shows a Handler callback in a live process.
  4. How I'd verify each: Repro: open the coupon screen, press back within 3 s, and it crashes. A unit or Robolectric test with FragmentScenario.moveToState(DESTROYED), then shadowOf(getMainLooper()).idle(). Check the git blame for the lazy's first-access line.
  5. Root cause: by viewModels() is a ViewModelLazy. Nothing is resolved until .value is first read. Before 6.4 that happened in onViewCreated, while the Fragment was attached. In 6.4 the first read moved into a postDelayed runnable. View.postDelayed posts to the main Handler, and removing the view does not remove the runnable. Strictly, View.removeCallbacks exists, and post on a detached view queues via ViewRootImpl's run queue. Either way, nothing here removed the runnable. When it fires after onDestroy, the lazy tries to resolve the store from a detached Fragment and throws. Even if vm had been initialized earlier, calling expireCoupon() on a cleared VM would be a silent logic bug.
  6. Fix: Short term: move the timing into the ViewModel, where it belongs, and make the UI only observe.
// ViewModel owns the timer: cancelled automatically in onCleared via viewModelScope
fun onCouponShown() {
    viewModelScope.launch {
        delay(3_000)
        expireCoupon()
    }
}

// Fragment: touch vm only inside the view lifecycle
override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    vm.onCouponShown()
}

If something must stay in the UI layer, use viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch { delay(3_000); ... }. It is cancelled at onDestroyView, unlike postDelayed. Long term: a review rule that Fragment code doesn't use Handler/postDelayed for logic, and an eager first access of delegates in onViewCreated if a screen relies on them. 7. Prevention: A lint check for postDelayed/Handler().post in Fragments. A FragmentScenario test that destroys the Fragment while a timer is pending. A Crashlytics velocity alert on new IllegalStateException signatures per release. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): No if (isAdded) guard as the fix. It hides the race and leaves the runnable holding the Fragment for 3 s, which is a short leak. No by lazy-style eager init in field initializers either: those run before attach and crash with the same exception.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Same scenario with by navArgs()? → NavArgsLazy reads arguments, which survive detach. It might not crash, but you're still running logic for a dead screen.
  • What if the delayed code were findNavController().navigate(...)? → After detach it throws IllegalStateException ("not associated with a NavController" or "does not have a NavController set"). Same root cause.
  • Why didn't viewModelScope have this problem? → It's cancelled in onCleared, so the delay is cancelled with the screen. Structured concurrency removes the race.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "delay then do something" pattern via postDelayed existed in nine Fragments. It only became a crash when a refactor made one of them the first touch of a lazy delegate. Moving timers into ViewModels removed the whole class of bug.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: isAdded check or a Hilt rollback with no mechanism.
  • Hire: explains lazy resolution timing plus the runnable outliving the Fragment, and moves the timer to a lifecycle-aware scope.
  • Strong hire: also uses breadcrumbs and device mix as evidence, dismisses the Hilt red herring with stack evidence, adds a lint rule and a FragmentScenario test, and notes the silent logic bug even when no crash happens.

questions.contextHtml: The app has a Settings class with 45 properties like var darkMode by prefs.boolean("dark_mode", false), built on a custom ReadWriteProperty over SharedPreferences. It is read from 120 call sites, including Compose code and Application.onCreate. Android vitals: ANR rate 0.41% (the bad-behaviour threshold is 0.47%). The top ANR cluster is in QueuedWork.waitToFinish during Activity.onStop, and StrictMode in debug flags DiskReadViolation from Settings.getDarkMode. The team wants to "move to DataStore but keep the nice by syntax."
questions.promptHtml: Evaluate the current delegate design, then decide how to migrate. Can you keep var x by ... on top of DataStore?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make the DataStore delegate call runBlocking { dataStore.data.first() } in getValue." That keeps the syntax and moves the disk read onto the main thread behind a coroutine facade, which is worse than SharedPreferences, because SP at least caches in memory.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which properties are read on startup or the main thread, versus rarely? Are writes apply() or commit()? Is any setting read from multiple processes? (SP MODE_MULTI_PROCESS is deprecated; DataStore has a MultiProcessDataStoreFactory.) Do UI layers need to observe changes or just read once?
  2. Immediate mitigation: The QueuedWork ANRs come from many apply() calls queued and then flushed synchronously in onStop. Batch writes into one edit { } and stop writing settings on every keystroke. Also preload SP on a background thread at startup (getSharedPreferences starts an async load, but the first get blocks until the file is loaded).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (for the ANR): (a) Bursts of apply() writes flushed on onStop, which is the main cluster. (b) First read on main waits for the SP file load, which is the StrictMode violation. (c) A large SP file (JSON blobs in prefs) makes both slower. Check the file size.
  4. How I'd verify each: ANR traces grouped by QueuedWork.waitToFinish. Perfetto at startup: look for the main thread blocked on SharedPreferencesImpl.awaitLoadedLocked. adb shell run-as to measure the prefs XML size. Count writes per session with a debug counter in setValue.
  5. Root cause: A synchronous property delegate is a synchronous API. It promises that getValue returns now. Over SharedPreferences that's mostly an in-memory map read, except for the first load and the apply() flush semantics. DataStore is deliberately asynchronous (Flow reads, suspend writes). A property getter can't suspend, so a DataStore-backed by can only be honest if it reads an in-memory snapshot that something else keeps up to date.
  6. Fix: Short term: keep the SP delegates, batch writes, move startup reads off main, and remove blobs. Long term: change the API shape, not the syntax.
class SettingsRepository(private val store: DataStore<Preferences>, appScope: CoroutineScope) {
    private val DARK = booleanPreferencesKey("dark_mode")

    val settings: StateFlow<Settings?> = store.data
        .map { Settings(darkMode = it[DARK] ?: false) }
        .stateIn(appScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, null) // null = not loaded yet: callers must handle it

    suspend fun setDarkMode(v: Boolean) { store.edit { it[DARK] = v } }
}

UI code collects settings. Imperative code that truly needs a snapshot reads settings.value, which is explicit about "may not be loaded". Migrate with DataStore's SharedPreferencesMigration, one group of keys at a time, behind a flag. 7. Prevention: StrictMode detectDiskReads as a CI failure for instrumentation tests. A lint ban on runBlocking in production source sets. A write-frequency budget on settings. An ANR dashboard split by top frame. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't hide runBlocking inside getValue: ANRs and deadlock risk on main. I wouldn't keep a read-only by over the StateFlow snapshot that throws or returns a default before load. That silently returns wrong values on cold start. I'd accept losing the var x by ergonomics, because the honest API is asynchronous.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can a delegate over StateFlow<Settings?>.value be acceptable? → Yes, for non-critical reads, if it is read-only and documented as "snapshot, may be default before load". Writes still need to go through a suspend function.
  • Is SharedPreferences apply() safe because it's async? → The write is async, but the Activity/Service lifecycle waits for pending writes in QueuedWork, which is how you get ANRs at onStop.
  • Proto DataStore or Preferences DataStore? → Proto for a typed schema and atomic multi-field updates. Preferences DataStore for a flat key-value set migrated from SP.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A settings screen wrote to prefs on every slider tick, about 60 apply()s per second. Leaving the screen flushed them all in onStop and accounted for most of the app's ANRs. Debouncing writes and batching into a single edit cleared the cluster before any DataStore migration started.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: runBlocking in the delegate to keep the syntax.
  • Hire: identifies the sync-vs-async mismatch and moves to Flow/suspend with SharedPreferencesMigration.
  • Strong hire: also diagnoses the QueuedWork ANR mechanism with traces, gives immediate mitigations without a migration, designs an explicit "not loaded" state, and stages the migration behind a flag.

questions.contextHtml: A feature module :payments reads PaymentConfig.MAX_RETRIES from the :core-config module. Last Tuesday :core-config changed const val MAX_RETRIES = 3 to 5, and CI went green. Production telemetry still shows the checkout flow retrying exactly 3 times for 18% of sessions. Those sessions are all on build 8.12.0, shipped from the release branch. Sessions on 8.12.1 (built on a different CI agent) retry 5 times. Crashes are flat. The backend team claims "the server rate limiter changed that week" (red herring).
questions.promptHtml: Explain how one source value yields two behaviours in the same release line, and fix both the immediate issue and the process.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Cache issue on the client, ask users to clear data", or blames remote config. It never considers that the value is copied into the other module's bytecode at compile time.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do the two builds come from different CI agents or caches? Is :core-config consumed as a project dependency or as a prebuilt artifact (AAR from an internal Maven)? Is Gradle remote build cache enabled? Is the constant used in an annotation or when branch?
  2. Immediate mitigation: The retry count is behaviour, not safety. If it's urgent, ship the value via remote config override. Otherwise rebuild :payments and release 8.12.2 from a clean build.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) const val was inlined into :payments bytecode, and :payments was restored from the build cache or a prebuilt artifact compiled before the change. (b) Remote config override: contradicted, because the same config reaches both builds. (c) Server-side rate limiting: would change responses, not the client retry count in logs.
  4. How I'd verify each: Decompile the release APK's :payments class (jadx, or Kotlin Bytecode viewer): if (attempt < 3) appears as a literal with no field reference. Compare the :payments class hash between 8.12.0 and 8.12.1. Check the Gradle build scan for :payments:compileReleaseKotlin FROM-CACHE on the 8.12.0 build. Check whether the cache key included the :core-config ABI.
  5. Root cause: const val is a compile-time constant that the compiler copies into every use site. A change to the constant is a change to dependents' bytecode, so correct builds must recompile them. Gradle normally does this, because the constant is part of the module's ABI. The bad build used a prebuilt :core-config artifact pinned to an older snapshot from the internal repository, and the :payments compile output was reused. The artifact still contained 3, so the literal 3 stayed in :payments, while the new :core-config code contained 5.
  6. Fix: Short term: clean rebuild, republish, release. Long term: don't use const for values that can change independently of the consumers.
object PaymentConfig {
    // not inlined into consumers: read through the getter at runtime
    val MAX_RETRIES: Int get() = 5
    // or @JvmField val MAX_RETRIES = 5 (field read, still not inlined)
}

Even better, drive tunable values through remote config with a safe default, so they don't need a release. 7. Prevention: Keep const for true constants (HTTP status, JSON keys, annotation arguments). Pin library versions and don't consume snapshot artifacts for release builds. Add a CI check that release builds run with a clean cache for changed modules, or that cache keys include dependency ABIs. Add a binary-compatibility validator (binary-compatibility-validator plugin) to flag changes in public API dumps, which include constant values. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't turn the cache off globally, because it costs build time for everyone. I wouldn't change the value to 5 "again" to force a rebuild. It leaves the root cause. I wouldn't blame remote config before reading bytecode.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does the same happen with BuildConfig fields? → Yes. They are static final constants and are inlined into modules that read them, so the same caching rule applies. Different modules can disagree about BuildConfig.DEBUG if built separately.
  • Does @JvmField val x = 5 avoid it? → The consumer reads the field at runtime, so it sees the library's value. A Java compiler may still treat static final primitives with constant initializers as constants, so for Java callers of a library prefer a getter.
  • How does inline fun compare? → Public inline functions copy their body into callers the same way. A library change doesn't reach consumers until they recompile (see the inline chunk).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A published SDK shipped const val API_VERSION = "v2". A hotfix bumped it to "v3", but three client apps with a pre-built internal AAR kept sending "v2" for months. The fix was a getter and a contract test against the real endpoint.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames cache or backend with no bytecode evidence.
  • Hire: explains const inlining and the stale prebuilt module, fixes by removing const.
  • Strong hire: proves it by decompiling both builds, finds the CI cache/artifact cause, and adds ABI-diff and snapshot-dependency prevention.

questions.promptHtml: How does var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) } work as a delegated property, and what goes wrong when you use it incorrectly, for example inside a lambda or when the state is created outside composition?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Compose's most common line is a delegated property. Seniors can say exactly which part is remember, which part is by, and what reads and writes the snapshot system.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: mutableStateOf(0) creates a MutableState<Int>. remember { } caches that object across recompositions in the composition's slot table. by is the property delegate: androidx.compose.runtime provides inline extension operators State<T>.getValue and MutableState<T>.setValue, which read and write .value. The read goes through the snapshot system, which records "this composition scope read this state". A later write invalidates that scope. So by is only syntax. The behaviour comes from .value access, and the delegation is resolved at compile time with no delegate object per property.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Desugared:
val count$delegate: MutableState<Int> = remember { mutableStateOf(0) }
// reads:  count$delegate.getValue(null, ::count) -> count$delegate.value
// writes: count$delegate.setValue(null, ::count, v) -> count$delegate.value = v

These are local delegated properties (Q176). The getValue/setValue extensions are inline and ignore the KProperty argument, so there's no reflection and, when inlined, no extra call.

  • What is tracked: the snapshot read observer records that the current recompose scope read the state. A write inside a snapshot marks the state's readers as invalid, so those scopes recompose.
  • Common failure modes:
Mistake What happens
var x by mutableStateOf(0) without remember in a composable a new state each recomposition, so the value resets to 0 and the UI never "sticks"
Reading x in a deferred lambda (onClick = { x++ }) fine: it's a write/read at event time, with no composition tracking
Reading x in a parent just to pass it down the parent recomposes on every change. Pass a lambda ({ x }) or hoist, to narrow invalidation
Capturing x (the delegated value) in a long-lived coroutine you get the current Int each time the property is read, which is correct. But val snapshot = x copies the Int and goes stale
rememberSaveable needed remember is lost on config change/process death, rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(..) } isn't, if the type is Saveable
Mutable collection inside state (mutableStateOf(mutableListOf())) in-place .add() doesn't write .value, so there's no invalidation. Use mutableStateListOf or replace the list
  • Class-level version: var query by mutableStateOf("") as a property of a state-holder class works without remember, since the object itself is remembered by its owner (a ViewModel or remember { SearchState() }).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Counter() {
    var count by remember { mutableIntStateOf(0) }   // IntState avoids boxing; same delegate syntax
    Button(onClick = { count++ }) { Text("Clicked $count") }
}

class SearchState {
    var query by mutableStateOf("")          // delegate lives in the object, no remember needed here
        private set
    fun onQueryChange(q: String) { query = q }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting remember, so the counter resets.
  • Passing count (the Int) down instead of a lambda, which causes unneeded recompositions.
  • Using remember for state that must survive rotation or process death.
  • Assuming by allocates a delegate and is slow. It's an inline call on the state object that already exists.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. mutableIntStateOf vs mutableStateOf(0)? → mutableIntStateOf (Compose 1.5+) stores a primitive int and avoids boxing. The delegate syntax is the same, because IntState/MutableIntState have their own getValue/setValue.
  2. Why can't I use by on a StateFlow? → There's no getValue extension for it, and you don't want one: it would read a value without subscribing. Use collectAsStateWithLifecycle(), which returns a State and does subscribe.
  3. Is a snapshot write from a background thread safe? → Writes to snapshot state from any thread are allowed. Visibility to composition happens through snapshot apply, so ordering is defined by the snapshot system. That's not the same as being atomic for compound updates. For read-modify-write from multiple threads use update on a StateFlow or a Mutex.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "by lets me skip .value". The senior answer explains remember vs by vs snapshot tracking, the desugared form, the inline operators (no reflection), where reads should happen to limit recomposition, and rememberSaveable.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A screen kept var items by remember { mutableStateOf(mutableListOf<Row>()) } and called items.add(row). The UI never updated until an unrelated recomposition, and QA called it "flaky". Switching to mutableStateListOf fixed it.

questions.contextHtml:
App on 4M DAU. ANR rate rose from 0.22% to 0.55% (threshold 0.47%) after release 9.3. Top ANR cluster (about 60%): main thread blocked in SynchronizedLazyImpl.getValue inside CartProvider, while a DefaultDispatcher-worker-3 thread is blocked in SynchronizedLazyImpl.getValue inside PricingEngine. Thread dump excerpt:

"main" prio=5 tid=1 Blocked
  at com.app.PricingEngine$Companion.getRules (PricingEngine.kt:21)   // waiting for monitor held by worker-3
  at com.app.CartProvider.<init>(CartProvider.kt:14)
"DefaultDispatcher-worker-3" Blocked
  at com.app.CartProvider.getInstance (CartProvider.kt:30)          // waiting for monitor held by main
  at com.app.PricingEngine$rules$2.invoke (PricingEngine.kt:25)

Only a few percent of cold starts hit it, mostly on 4-core devices. A reviewer suspects the new analytics SDK (red herring).
questions.promptHtml: Explain the deadlock, how you'd confirm it, and fix it without making startup slower.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Move the work to a background thread" or "use lazy(NONE)". The first doesn't remove the circular dependency. The second removes the lock and the exactly-once guarantee, so it trades a deadlock for a race.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed in 9.3 (a new pre-warm of PricingEngine on Dispatchers.Default)? Are the two lazies in a dependency cycle by design? Are both in object/companion (static singletons)? Why only some cold starts (timing)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the pre-warm via remote config, or stage a hotfix removing the Default call. That removes the second thread and the cycle can't deadlock.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A lock-ordering deadlock: main holds CartProvider's lazy lock and wants PricingEngine's, and worker-3 holds PricingEngine's and wants CartProvider's. (b) The SDK blocks main: contradicted, since the dump shows both threads in our lazies. (c) Class-initialization (<clinit>) deadlock: possible in the same shape, but frames show SynchronizedLazyImpl, so it's lazy monitors.
  4. How I'd verify each: Read Blocked threads in the ANR trace and follow the "waiting to lock <0x...> held by tid=N" chain, which closes a cycle. Reproduce with a unit test that starts two threads touching the two properties in opposite order with a CountDownLatch to line them up. The Android Studio thread dump shows the same cycle on a debug build.
  5. Root cause: Two SYNCHRONIZED lazies whose initializers depend on each other, both reachable from different threads. Main initializes CartProvider.instance, taking its lock, and in its initializer reads PricingEngine.rules. The pre-warm thread is already inside PricingEngine.rules, holding that lock, and its initializer reads CartProvider.getInstance(). Each waits for the other. It's a classic two-lock cycle, hidden because lazy makes the locks invisible. It depends on timing, which explains the low rate.
  6. Fix: Short term: break the cycle by having PricingEngine not read CartProvider during initialization (pass what it needs as a parameter, or read it lazily at call time).
class PricingEngine(private val cart: Provider<Cart>) { // inject a Provider, no init-time cycle
    val rules by lazy { loadRules() }                    // loadRules() no longer touches Cart
    fun price(): Money = compute(cart.get(), rules)
}

Long term: constructor-inject with Hilt (a cycle becomes a compile-time error, or Provider/Lazy makes it explicit), keep initializers small, with no cross-singleton calls, and run startup-critical initializers in one place with a defined order (App Startup Initializer dependencies). 7. Prevention: Start-up thread-dump test in CI (cold start with StrictMode and a deliberate pre-warm). A lint rule/review guideline: lazy initializers must not call other singletons' lazies. A watchdog (ANRWatchDog debug) that dumps threads at 2 s main-thread stalls. Track "main blocked on monitor" in Perfetto traces. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't use PUBLICATION. It avoids the lock but may run the initializer twice concurrently, and each initializer that reads the other's lazy would still recurse. I wouldn't wrap it in a timeout. I wouldn't add more pre-warming to "hide" the stall.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does reentrancy on one lazy not deadlock but recurse? → The monitor is reentrant, so the same thread re-enters, still sees UNINITIALIZED, and calls the initializer again. You get a StackOverflowError, not a deadlock.
  • Same bug with top-level vals in two files? → The JVM class-init locks can deadlock the same way: thread A initializes AKt needing BKt, thread B initializes BKt needing AKt.
  • Could coroutines make it worse? → Yes. Blocking inside a Default worker holds one of a few threads while waiting for a lock held by a thread waiting on that dispatcher, which is lock plus starvation.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "faster startup" change pre-warmed three singletons on a background pool. It exposed a two-singleton cycle that had been safe only because everything ran on main, which serialised it. The deadlock only reproduced on devices where the pool thread won the race.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: switches to NONE or just moves work to a thread.
  • Hire: reads the dump, finds the lock cycle between lazies, and breaks the dependency.
  • Strong hire: also explains why it's timing-dependent, relates it to class-init deadlocks and dispatcher starvation, and proposes DI-level and CI-level prevention.

questions.contextHtml: Post-incident review. An AuditedPaymentGateway decorates PaymentGateway using class AuditedPaymentGateway(private val real: PaymentGateway, private val audit: AuditLog) : PaymentGateway by real. It overrides charge() to write an audit record. Release 7.2 added fun chargeWithToken(token: String, cents: Long) to the PaymentGateway interface for a new checkout. The new method went through the decorator via compiler-generated forwarding, so 41k payments (about 6% of transactions over 9 days) were charged with no audit record. No crash, no failed tests: the new method was covered by gateway tests but not by decorator tests. Finance noticed a reconciliation gap.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: causes, contributing factors, what you'd change in code and process.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add the missing override and be more careful." It treats the incident as human error and not as a design property of by plus a growing interface.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the audit a compliance requirement or a diagnostic? (Compliance, so the failure mode matters.) Which other decorators wrap this interface? Was there any signal when the interface changed (compile error, test failure, review comment)? How was the gap detected, and how late?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Override chargeWithToken with the audit call and release. Backfill the audit table from payment provider settlement records for the 9 days. Notify compliance. Add a temporary reconciliation alert for "payment without audit row".
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (contributing factors): (a) by silently forwards new interface members, so adding a method produced valid code with the wrong behaviour. (b) The cross-cutting concern was implemented per method, not at a single choke point. (c) No test asserts "every PaymentGateway method writes an audit". (d) Review process: the PR touching the interface didn't list implementers and wrappers.
  4. How I'd verify each: Diff the 7.1 and 7.2 PaymentGateway. Use "Find usages / implementations" to list the wrappers. Run a reflection test over PaymentGateway::class.members that calls each method through the decorator with a fake AuditLog and counts records. It fails before the fix.
  5. Root cause: Class delegation forwards every member the class doesn't override, including ones added later. For a pass-through wrapper that's the feature. For an enforcing wrapper (audit, auth, redaction) it's the hazard, because the safe default for a new method is "intercepted", while the generated default is "bypassed". The incident is a missing-override failure that the compiler can't see.
  6. Fix: Short term: add the override. Medium term: invert the default so new members can't bypass by accident:
// Option A: a single choke point the interface itself provides
interface PaymentGateway {
    fun charge(req: ChargeRequest): Result
    fun chargeWithToken(token: String, cents: Long): Result = charge(ChargeRequest.fromToken(token, cents)) // all paths end in charge()
}
// the decorator audits only charge(); chargeWithToken's default calls it on the same wrapper
// BUT only if the decorator implements the interface WITHOUT forwarding that default (see below)

// Option B: don't use 'by' for enforcing wrappers; implement every member explicitly,
// so the compiler errors on any newly added abstract member:
class AuditedPaymentGateway(private val real: PaymentGateway, private val audit: AuditLog) : PaymentGateway {
    override fun charge(req: ChargeRequest) = audit.around(req) { real.charge(req) }
    override fun chargeWithToken(token: String, cents: Long) = audit.around(token) { real.chargeWithToken(token, cents) }
}

A caveat on option A: with by real, a default method is forwarded to real's implementation (the default runs on real, calling real.charge, not the decorator's). So the audit would still be bypassed. That's the self-call limitation from Q174. That's why option B, explicit implementation, is the safe choice for enforcing wrappers. Another approach is to make the real gateway take an AuditLog and audit internally, so it can't be bypassed from outside. 7. Prevention: For enforcement decorators: no by. Explicit overrides, so interface changes break the build. A contract test that iterates all interface methods through the decorator. An invariant check in production: a reconciliation job comparing payments to audit rows with alerting. A PR template checkbox, "implementations and wrappers reviewed", for changes to core interfaces. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't ban by in general: for pass-through wrappers (caching, metrics, test fakes) it's great. I wouldn't depend on reviewers remembering. I wouldn't rely on reflection tests alone: a compile error is stronger than a test.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would a sealed interface or abstract class help? → An abstract class with abstract members forces subclasses to implement them. But Kotlin by works with interfaces only, so explicit implementation is the equivalent.
  • A Java dynamic Proxy for auditing every call? → It intercepts every method, including new ones, so it fits enforcement. The cost is reflection, harder stack traces and R8 keep rules.
  • How do you catch this in code review automatically? → A custom detekt rule: flag : SomeInterface by x where the interface name is on a "must intercept" list.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rate-limiting wrapper over a network client used by. A new bulk endpoint was added to the interface and ran unthrottled for a week until the backend's own limits hit. The fix replaced by with explicit implementation plus a test that enumerated interface methods.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "be more careful" or only adds the missing override.
  • Hire: identifies silent forwarding as the mechanism and replaces by with explicit overrides or an internal choke point.
  • Strong hire: also notes the default-method self-call limitation, adds contract tests and reconciliation monitoring, handles backfill and compliance communication, and separates pass-through from enforcing decorators.

questions.contextHtml: An e-commerce app (single Activity, 14 Fragments) uses private val shared: AppStateViewModel by activityViewModels() in 9 Fragments as a convenient shared store. It holds the cart, selected address, applied coupon, filters and the last search results (about 1.8 MB of parsed product models). Symptoms: after completing checkout and starting a new one, the old coupon appears pre-applied (QA: "ghost coupon"). Memory profiler shows the retained size of AppStateViewModel at 14 MB after a long session. TransactionTooLargeException appears in some onSaveInstanceState paths (0.02% sessions). Crash-free is 99.6%. Product wants a "guest checkout" flow that can open from three entry points, and for the cart to survive process death.
questions.promptHtml: Critique the design and propose a scoping and state-persistence plan, with a migration path that doesn't stop feature work.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a reset() method and call it after checkout." It treats the scoping problem as a missing cleanup call, and keeps one VM for everything.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which state truly lives for the whole session (cart, auth) and which belongs to a flow (checkout address, coupon)? What must survive process death (cart yes, search results no)? Do any screens need to be reachable from multiple graphs? Is the cart persisted server-side or locally?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the ghost coupon with an explicit clear on checkout completion, tracked with a ticket to remove it. Drop the search results from the shared VM (fetch/paging per screen) to relieve memory. That's a small PR.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (for the symptoms): (a) Activity-scoped VM outlives the logical flow, so flow state leaks between runs (ghost coupon). (b) Large result lists in a long-lived VM cause the 14 MB retention. (c) TransactionTooLargeException comes from putting big objects into SavedStateHandle/Bundles. Check, since saved state is limited to roughly 1 MB per transaction across the process.
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap dump (Android Studio): dominator tree under AppStateViewModel. Log VM identity hash across two checkouts. Inspect SavedStateHandle keys and sizes in a debug build (Bundle parcel size via Parcel.obtain().dataSize()), and the TransactionTooLargeException stack for the offending Bundle.
  5. Root cause: The scope is the lifetime. activityViewModels ties state to the Activity, which in a single-Activity app is effectively the whole session. Flow-local state in it never gets cleared by the framework, so correctness depends on every exit path calling a manual cleanup. A single "god" store also couples nine screens through one mutable object, and mixes data with different lifetimes (cart: persistent, coupon: per checkout, search results: per screen).
  6. Fix: Scope each piece of state to its real owner:
State Owner Why
Cart repository (Room, singleton) exposed as Flow survives process death, shared by all screens
Checkout flow (address, coupon, payment choice) hiltNavGraphViewModels(R.id.checkout_graph) cleared automatically when the graph is popped, so no ghost coupon
Search results screen ViewModel with Paging per screen, not retained after leaving
Screen inputs (query, selected tab) SavedStateHandle (small primitives only) survive process death within the limit 
@AndroidEntryPoint
class PaymentFragment : Fragment(R.layout.payment) {
    private val checkout: CheckoutViewModel by hiltNavGraphViewModels(R.id.checkout_graph)
}

Guest checkout from three entry points: each entry navigates into the same nested graph (<include> or a shared navigation destination), so the VM scope is the graph, not the caller. Migration: introduce CheckoutViewModel beside the old VM, move one field group per PR, and delete fields from AppStateViewModel as they move. Keep feature work flowing by making each PR behaviour-neutral. 7. Prevention: A guideline: activityViewModels only for state that truly spans the Activity (e.g., a toolbar or a session snapshot), reviewed in PRs. A test that finishes the checkout graph and asserts a fresh CheckoutViewModel instance on the second entry. A max-size assertion on Bundles in debug. A leak/heap budget in a nightly Macrobenchmark run. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't create a global singleton "app state" object instead: that removes lifecycle entirely and worsens the leak. I wouldn't put the cart in SavedStateHandle. It's the wrong size and the wrong persistence layer: the cart belongs in Room. I wouldn't do a big-bang rewrite when incremental extraction works.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the checkout graph must also be launchable from a deep link? → A nested graph works with deep links, and the NavBackStackEntry for the graph is created on entry. Make sure required inputs come from the deep-link arguments, not from the old shared VM.
  • Compose Navigation equivalent? → hiltViewModel(navController.getBackStackEntry("checkout")), or the type-safe route class in newer Navigation versions. The VM is scoped to the back stack entry.
  • Process death mid-checkout? → SavedStateHandle restores small inputs. Larger drafts go into Room with a draft id, so the VM re-reads by id.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shared "UiStateViewModel" grew over two years to 60 fields. A heap dump showed it retained a whole product catalog page after the user left the catalog. Splitting by lifetime into flow-scoped, screen-scoped and repository-owned state cut retained memory by about 10 MB and removed a family of "stale data" bugs.

• No hire: adds reset() and keeps one shared VM.
  • Hire: maps each piece of state to a proper scope (nav graph, screen, repository) and fixes the ghost coupon structurally.
  • Strong hire: also quantifies retention and saved-state limits, uses Room for process-death survival, designs the multi-entry guest flow, and plans an incremental, behaviour-neutral migration with tests and guidelines.
